title: A relaxation system for the low-Mach limit of kinetic equations: Stability and higher order asymptotic preserving scheme
summary: This work introduces a hyperbolic relaxation system designed for the simulation of kinetic equations in the low-Mach number limit. The methodology is built upon a micro-macro decomposition of the scaled BGK model, which reformulates the kinetic distribution function into a coupled system consisting of a macroscopic equilibrium part and a microscopic non-equilibrium remainder. By projecting the microscopic deviations onto a set of orthogonal polynomials, we derive a closed moment relaxation system. The resulting system is a version of Grad's 13 moment system with a linear hyperbolic part and a relaxation adapted to the incompressible limit. We prove the model's structural stability in the incompressible Navier-Stokes limit. Moreover, we develop a high order Asymptotic-Preserving (AP) numerical framework using Implicit-Explicit (IMEX) Runge Kutta schemes for temporal accuracy and finite difference WENO reconstructions as well as central difference approximations for high order spatial resolution. The proposed scheme ensures uniform stability and consistency across different physical regimes, automatically degenerating into a consistent high order discretization of the incompressible thermal Navier-Stokes limit as the scaling parameter vanishes. Numerical experiments in one and two dimensions corroborate the theoretical findings, demonstrating significant reductions in computational cost and robust performance across a wide range of Knudsen and Mach numbers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hyperbolic relaxation system for simulating kinetic equations in the low-Mach number limit, based on micro-macro decomposition of the BGK model, with an Asymptotic-Preserving IMEX/WENO numerical framework.
AI.motivation: Simulating kinetic equations in the low-Mach number limit is challenging due to stiffness and the need for schemes that remain accurate and stable across diverse physical regimes (varying Knudsen and Mach numbers).
AI.method: A micro-macro decomposition of the scaled BGK model splits the distribution into macroscopic equilibrium and microscopic non-equilibrium parts. Projecting microscopic deviations onto orthogonal polynomials yields a closed moment relaxation system—a Grad's 13-moment-type system with linear hyperbolic part and relaxation adapted to the incompressible limit. A high-order AP framework uses IMEX Runge-Kutta for time and finite difference WENO plus central differences for space.
AI.result: Structural stability in the incompressible Navier-Stokes limit is proved. The scheme maintains uniform stability and consistency across regimes, degenerating into a consistent high-order discretization of the incompressible thermal Navier-Stokes limit as the scaling parameter vanishes. 1D and 2D experiments confirm theory, showing large computational cost reductions and robust performance across wide Knudsen and Mach number ranges.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hyperbolic relaxation system and AP numerical framework provide an efficient, stable, and accurate approach for kinetic simulations in the low-Mach limit.

title: Matrix-Free Moment-Matching Method for Reduced-Order Modeling of Quadratic-Bilinear Descriptor Systems with Multiple Inputs
summary: This paper develops a new moment-matching order reduction method for multi-input quadratic-bilinear descriptor systems. The proposed approach accommodates multiple inputs acting on both the differential and algebraic equations and constructs separate projection spaces associated with different input channels and input combinations. The method uses a matrix-free algorithm, allowing the reduced-order matrices and tensors to be computed without explicitly assembling or storing the full-order system matrices and tensors. This feature makes the proposed method particularly suitable for large-scale computational fluid dynamics problems. Numerical experiments carried out for two-dimensional flow problems demonstrate that the resulting reduced-order models accurately reproduce the transient responses of the full-order models under multiple time-varying inputs.

AI.tldr: A matrix-free moment-matching model order reduction method for multi-input quadratic-bilinear descriptor systems, validated on 2D flow problems.
AI.motivation: Large-scale systems like computational fluid dynamics problems are expensive to simulate. Existing order reduction methods struggle with multi-input quadratic-bilinear descriptor systems where inputs act on both differential and algebraic equations.
AI.method: A moment-matching order reduction method that accommodates multiple inputs acting on both differential and algebraic equations, constructs separate projection spaces for different input channels and input combinations, and uses a matrix-free algorithm avoiding explicit assembly/storage of full-order matrices and tensors.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on 2D flow problems show the reduced-order models accurately reproduce transient responses of full-order models under multiple time-varying inputs.
AI.conclusion: The method is well-suited for large-scale CFD problems, enabling efficient and accurate reduction of multi-input quadratic-bilinear descriptor systems.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Landweber Iteration with Randomized Normal-Operator Approximation
summary: Iterative methods are extremely popular for solving linear ill-posed inverse problems. While deterministic convergence, or more precisely, semi-convergence of such methods is widely studied, the problem of quantifying uncertainty in the resulting reconstructions due to random noise in the observed data has received far less attention. In this work, we study uncertainty quantification for the Landweber iteration in linear inverse problems using the Radon transform as a motivating example. We interpret the Landweber reconstruction statistically by analyzing how uncertainty in the measured data is propagated through the reconstruction map. This perspective is closely related to generalized fiducial inference, where uncertainty about the parameter is induced by inverting the relation between the observed data and the unknown (fixed) quantity. We combine the resulting stochastic uncertainty with a theoretical bound on the regularization bias to construct confidence intervals for the reconstructed solution. The evaluation of the resulting uncertainty estimates require repeated operations with the forward operator that can become expensive in large-scale problems. To reduce this cost, we use randomized singular value decomposition to obtain a low-rank approximation of the normal operator associated with the Radon transform and incorporate this approximation in quantifying uncertainty. {In particular, this requires that the additional randomization error introduced due to the use of such randomized techniques be included in our approach for uncertainty quantification.} Numerical results show that the proposed method provides accurate reconstructions and reliable uncertainty estimates at substantially reduced computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper develops uncertainty quantification for the Landweber iteration in linear ill-posed inverse problems (motivated by the Radon transform), combining generalized fiducial inference with a regularization bias bound to build confidence intervals, and uses randomized SVD for computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Deterministic convergence (semi-convergence) of iterative methods for linear ill-posed inverse problems is well studied, but quantifying uncertainty in reconstructions caused by random noise in observed data has received far less attention.
AI.method: The Landweber reconstruction is interpreted statistically by propagating data uncertainty through the reconstruction map, closely related to generalized fiducial inference. Stochastic uncertainty is combined with a theoretical regularization bias bound to construct confidence intervals. Randomized SVD gives a low-rank approximation of the normal operator for the Radon transform, incorporating the additional randomization error into the quantification.
AI.result: Numerical results show the proposed method provides accurate reconstructions and reliable uncertainty estimates at substantially reduced computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables statistically valid uncertainty quantification for iterative regularization in large-scale problems, with randomization error properly accounted for.

title: A Deferred Correction, Continuous Galerkin Method for Curvilinear Staggered-Grid Lagrangian Hydrodynamics
summary: We present a continuous Galerkin, Deferred Correction (cG-DeC) method for the equations of Lagrangian hydrodynamics. The proposed scheme combines a high-order continuous finite element discretization with an explicit Deferred Correction time integrator, yielding a formulation that avoids the inversion of a global sparse mass matrix at each update. To stabilize the method in the presence of strong shocks we introduce a modification of the hyperviscosity model that is compatible with the cG-DeC framework and likewise does not require a global solve to construct the finite element approximation to the polyharmonic operator. We further present an alternative reformulation of the DeC iteration which admits a simple recursive algorithmic structure and provides insight into previously observed convergence behavior of explicit DeC applied to hyperbolic partial differential equations. Conservation of momentum and total energy of the resulting fully discrete scheme is analyzed. A set of numerical experiments illustrates the accuracy and robustness of the cG-DeC scheme. Comparisons with a continuous Galerkin Runge-Kutta (cG-RK) method are provided.

AI.tldr: A continuous Galerkin Deferred Correction (cG-DeC) method for Lagrangian hydrodynamics that avoids solving a global mass matrix, with a modified hyperviscosity for shock stabilization.
AI.motivation: High-order Lagrangian hydrodynamics schemes typically require inverting a global sparse mass matrix each update, and explicit Deferred Correction (DeC) applied to hyperbolic PDEs has shown unclear convergence behavior; the authors aim to combine a high-order continuous finite element discretization with an explicit DeC time integrator to avoid global solves.
AI.method: Combines a high-order continuous finite element spatial discretization with an explicit Deferred Correction time integrator, avoiding inversion of a global sparse mass matrix. Introduces a hyperviscosity model modification compatible with cG-DeC that also avoids global solves for the polyharmonic operator approximation. Presents a reformulation of the DeC iteration with a simple recursive structure, and analyzes conservation of momentum and total energy.
AI.result: Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy and robustness of the cG-DeC scheme, with comparisons to a continuous Galerkin Runge-Kutta (cG-RK) method.
AI.conclusion: The cG-DeC scheme provides an accurate and robust high-order method for Lagrangian hydrodynamics without global mass-matrix solves, with the modified hyperviscosity stabilizing shocks and the recursive DeC reformulation offering insight into convergence behavior; momentum and total energy conservation are established.

title: From Energy-Force Weighting to Primal-Dual Optimization of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are commonly fitted by weighted-sum scalarization, which combines energy and force errors in a single loss. A nominal weight, however, identifies a potential only relative to the complete fitting protocol. We therefore treat energy--force balancing as a protocol-dependent problem of physical model selection. For fixed-basis atomic cluster expansion models of molten LiCl, liquid H$_2$O, and Si, the resulting scalarization paths contain dominated states at extreme weights. Their nondominated subsets depend on the solver, and the out-of-distribution Si path is nonmonotone. We replace direct weight selection by minimizing the regularized energy objective subject to an upper bound on the normalized force loss. Projected dual ascent adjusts the Lagrange multiplier from the force-constraint residual. A frozen-multiplier limited-memory quasi-Newton refinement then returns the final model. Across the three systems, the constrained procedure reaches the solver-matched low-error region and gives measured speedups of $6.7$--$8.9$ over completed scalarization scans under the stated timing convention. Physical-property calculations show that first-shell geometry is comparatively insensitive to the selected balance, whereas transport and solid-state observables vary more strongly. These results identify the fitted model--protocol pair as the relevant object of energy--force model selection and support force-constrained fitting as an explicit selection rule.

AI.tldr: Energy-force balancing in ML interatomic potentials is reframed as a protocol-dependent model-selection problem; a force-constrained optimization replaces weight scalarization, yielding solver-matched accuracy with 6.7-8.9x speedups.
AI.motivation: A nominal scalarization weight only identifies a potential relative to the full fitting protocol, making direct weight selection ambiguous and unreliable. The authors argue energy-force balancing should be treated as protocol-dependent physical model selection, and seek a principled selection rule that avoids dominated and solver-dependent states.
AI.method: The study fits fixed-basis atomic cluster expansion models for molten LiCl, liquid H2O, and Si. Instead of direct weight scalarization, they minimize a regularized energy objective subject to an upper bound on normalized force loss. Projected dual ascent updates the Lagrange multiplier from the force-constraint residual, followed by frozen-multiplier L-BFGS refinement.
AI.result: Scalarization paths contain dominated states at extreme weights, with nondominated subsets depending on the solver; the out-of-distribution Si path is nonmonotone. The constrained procedure reaches the solver-matched low-error region with 6.7-8.9x speedups over completed scalarization scans. First-shell geometry is relatively insensitive to balance, while transport and solid-state observables vary more strongly.
AI.conclusion: The fitted model-protocol pair is the relevant object for energy-force model selection, and force-constrained fitting is supported as an explicit, efficient selection rule.

title: Fusing Global Diagnostic Signals and Spectral Data for Electron and Ion Temperature Profile Prediction on EAST via Attention-based Neural Networks
summary: Ion temperature Ti and electron temperature Te are fundamental kinetic parameters for evaluating tokamak plasma confinement, turbulent transport and magnetohydrodynamic stability. Reliable prediction of their spatiotemporal profiles is essential for long-pulse steady-state operation on the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST). However, existing EAST diagnostic systems have obvious measurement limitations, including narrow applicable conditions of charge exchange recombination spectroscopy and severe signal degradation of edge temperature diagnostics during long discharges. Classical physics-based transport codes suffer from high computational cost and error accumulation, while existing data-driven models only separately predict Ti or Te relying on spectral data, lacking joint Ti/Te modeling and failing under missing spectral measurements. In this work, we propose a multi-modal (i.e., global macroscopic diagnostic signals and spectral data) fusion attention neural network for simultaneous reconstruction of Ti/Te profiles on EAST. It leverages an adaptive attention module to weight global diagnostic features and suppress noise interference, employs convolutional layers to extract deep spectral representations, and utilizes multi-head self-attention to facilitate cross-modal feature interaction. Two separate prediction heads are constructed to output full radial distributions of Ti and Te. This work builds the first EAST-oriented joint Ti/Te prediction model compatible with operating scenarios without spectral diagnostics. Hierarchical attention mechanisms excavate nonlinear multi-modal correlations to realize high-performance dual-temperature profile prediction. The source code of this paper is available on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenFusion/tree/main/TiTe_Prediction

AI.tldr: A multi-modal fusion attention neural network jointly reconstructs ion and electron temperature profiles on EAST, handling missing spectral diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Ti and Te are key kinetic parameters for tokamak confinement, transport and stability, but EAST diagnostics have limited applicability (narrow CXRS conditions, edge signal degradation), physics codes are costly with error accumulation, and existing data-driven models predict Ti or Te separately from spectra only, failing with missing spectral data.
AI.method: Multi-modal fusion attention network combining global macroscopic diagnostic signals and spectral data: adaptive attention module weights global diagnostic features and suppresses noise; convolutional layers extract deep spectral representations; multi-head self-attention enables cross-modal interaction; two separate prediction heads output full radial Ti and Te distributions.
AI.result: First EAST-oriented joint Ti/Te prediction model compatible with operating scenarios lacking spectral diagnostics; hierarchical attention exploits nonlinear multi-modal correlations for high-performance dual-temperature profile prediction.
AI.conclusion: The joint multi-modal model overcomes separate-prediction and missing-spectral-data limitations, enabling reliable simultaneous Ti/Te profile reconstruction for EAST long-pulse steady-state operation. Code available at the provided GitHub link.

title: Global Strong Solutions for the Ternary Maxwell-Stefan Diffusion System
summary: We prove global strong well-posedness for the normalized isothermal, isobaric ternary Maxwell-Stefan diffusion system on bounded $C^{2+α_0}$ domains, for arbitrary positive constant binary frictions and compatible nonnegative initial data, without a smallness condition. For distinct frictions, trace--determinant variables produce two separated spectral roots satisfying scalar parabolic equations with antisymmetric quadratic coupling. Euler-Poisson-Darboux one-sided truncations, stabilized by the mixing entropy, yield boundary De Giorgi oscillation decay and positive-time Hölder regularity. The mixing-entropy Hessian then provides a local symmetrizer; conormal Schauder estimates give uniform $C^{1+a}$ control, and frozen maximal $L_p$-regularity yields a uniform terminal trace bound excluding finite-time breakdown. Repeated frictions reduce to triangular scalar parabolic systems. Every component with positive conserved mass is strictly positive for positive time.

AI.tldr: The paper proves global strong well-posedness for the normalized isothermal, isobaric ternary Maxwell-Stefan diffusion system on bounded C^{2+α0} domains, for arbitrary positive binary frictions and compatible nonnegative initial data, with no smallness condition.
AI.motivation: To establish global well-posedness for the ternary Maxwell-Stefan diffusion system without restrictive smallness assumptions, handling degenerate and cross-diffusive couplings for general frictions and nonnegative data.
AI.method: Trace-determinant variables split the spectrum into two scalar parabolic equations with antisymmetric quadratic coupling (distinct frictions); Euler-Poisson-Darboux one-sided truncations stabilized by mixing entropy; boundary De Giorgi oscillation decay and positive-time Hölder regularity; a local symmetrizer from the mixing-entropy Hessian; conormal Schauder estimates for uniform C^{1+a} control; frozen maximal L_p-regularity for a uniform terminal trace bound.
AI.result: Global strong well-posedness with uniform C^{1+a} control, positive-time Hölder regularity, and no finite-time breakdown. Repeated frictions reduce to triangular scalar parabolic systems; every component with positive conserved mass stays strictly positive for positive time.
AI.conclusion: The ternary Maxwell-Stefan diffusion system is globally strongly well-posed under general compatible data, with strict positivity for components of positive conserved mass and no smallness requirement.

title: Positivity-preserving scalar auxiliary variable schemes for gradient flows via a quadratic reformulation
summary: The scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) method replaces the nonlinear part of the free energy by a positive scalar $r(t)=\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_{_\mathcal{N}}[φ]+C}>0$, thereby yielding linear, unconditionally energy-stable schemes for gradient flows. At the discrete level, however, the standard backward Euler and Crank--Nicolson discretizations provide no guarantee that the computed $r^{n+1}$ remains positive, an inconsistency with the continuous definition that contradicts the square-root ansatz and may compromise long-time robustness. Although the SAV method has been widely applied, this subtle but consequential issue has received little attention. We first characterize this failure quantitatively by deriving a sharp criterion and a sufficient condition on the time step size, and construct an explicit counterexample showing that sign loss occurs for parameters of practical relevance. Rather than modifying the definition of $r$ as in existing positivity-preserving variants, we retain the square-root form and reformulate the discrete evolution from $r_t$ to $(r^{2})_t$, which converts the scalar equation into a convex quadratic with a strictly negative constant term, always yielding a unique positive root. For the Crank--Nicolson scheme, the product-form discretization $r^{n+1}r^{n}$ preserves this quadratic structure, while conventional alternatives do not. The resulting schemes incur the same computational cost as the original SAV method and are proved unconditionally energy-stable. Numerical experiments for the Cahn--Hilliard equation confirm the predicted positivity, energy stability, and convergence rates.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and fixes a positivity failure in the scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) method for gradient flows: standard backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson discretizations can produce non-positive r^{n+1}. By reformulating the discrete evolution from r_t to (r^2)_t into a convex quadratic with a negative constant term, the authors obtain unconditionally energy-stable schemes with guaranteed positive roots at the same computational cost.
AI.motivation: The SAV method yields linear, unconditionally energy-stable schemes by replacing the nonlinear free-energy part with a positive scalar r(t)=sqrt(E_N[φ]+C). However, at the discrete level the standard backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson schemes do not guarantee that r^{n+1} stays positive, contradicting the square-root ansatz and potentially harming long-time robustness. This subtle yet consequential issue has received little attention.
AI.method: The authors first characterize the failure quantitatively via a sharp criterion and a sufficient condition on the time step, plus an explicit counterexample showing sign loss at practical parameters. Instead of modifying the definition of r as in existing positivity-preserving variants, they keep the square-root form and reformulate the discrete evolution from r_t to (r^2)_t, converting the scalar equation into a convex quadratic with a strictly negative constant term, which always admits a unique positive root. For Crank-Nicolson, a product-form discretization r^{n+1}r^{n} preserves this quadratic structure, whereas conventional alternatives do not.
AI.result: The resulting schemes have the same computational cost as the original SAV method and are proved unconditionally energy-stable. Numerical experiments on the Cahn-Hilliard equation confirm the predicted positivity, energy stability, and convergence rates. The analysis also provides a sharp criterion and sufficient time-step condition for positivity and an explicit counterexample of sign loss.
AI.conclusion: Positivity of r in discrete SAV schemes is not automatic; reformulating the scalar evolution in terms of (r^2)_t preserves the square-root ansatz while guaranteeing a unique positive root. The proposed backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson variants remain unconditionally energy-stable and cost-equivalent to standard SAV, offering improved long-time robustness.

title: Automated Many-Body Simulations of Strongly Correlated Systems Using a Correlation-Aware Agentic Framework
summary: We present CAFES, a correlation-aware agentic framework for electronic-structure simulations of strongly correlated systems. CAFES addresses two challenges: the fragmented software landscape for many-body calculations and the difficulty of selecting appropriate methods across diverse correlation regimes. It combines correlation diagnostics, adaptive method selection, and large language model (LLM) assistance for molecular, crystalline, and model-Hamiltonian systems. A study-task architecture separates study-level planning from task-level execution, while a curated scientific knowledge layer provides reusable guidance for method selection, workflow design, and result interpretation. We demonstrate CAFES through three research-level studies: calculating the low-lying electronic states of lutein using DMRG-CASSCF, probing phase competition in the extended honeycomb Hubbard model using DMET, and generating a quantum-chemical dataset with CCSD labels. These calculations demonstrate the potential of agentic workflows for strongly correlated electronic-structure problems, a regime that has received limited attention in existing agentic computational frameworks.

AI.tldr: CAFES is a correlation-aware agentic framework that combines correlation diagnostics, adaptive method selection, and LLM assistance for electronic-structure simulations of strongly correlated systems across molecular, crystalline, and model-Hamiltonian cases.
AI.motivation: Two challenges are addressed: the fragmented software landscape for many-body calculations, and the difficulty of selecting appropriate methods across diverse correlation regimes. Existing agentic computational frameworks have given limited attention to strongly correlated electronic-structure problems.
AI.method: A study-task architecture separates study-level planning from task-level execution, paired with a curated scientific knowledge layer offering reusable guidance for method selection, workflow design, and result interpretation. It integrates correlation diagnostics, adaptive method selection, and LLM assistance.
AI.result: Demonstrated via three research-level studies: low-lying electronic states of lutein using DMRG-CASSCF; phase competition in the extended honeycomb Hubbard model using DMET; and a quantum-chemical dataset with CCSD labels.
AI.conclusion: These calculations show the potential of agentic workflows for strongly correlated electronic-structure problems, a regime underexplored by existing agentic computational frameworks.

title: Nuclear Fusion Knowledge Graph Guided Edge-Localized Mode Recognition on EAST
summary: Edge-localized modes (ELMs) are transient magnetohydrodynamic instabilities commonly observed in tokamak plasmas. Although deep time-series models can learn complex dynamic patterns from multi-diagnostic signals, their predictions are mainly data-driven and lack explicit utilization of ELM physics, plasma operating states, and historical discharge experience. As a result, they may confuse categories with similar temporal patterns, particularly under severe class imbalance. To address this issue, we propose KGF-ELM, a Knowledge Graph Fusion Network for ELM Recognition, and introduce a Knowledge Graph Collaborative Fusion Module (KGCFM) that organizes physical evidence from the current time window, ELM prototypes, relational knowledge graph representations, and similar historical discharge cases into complementary multi-source knowledge representations. KGCFM collaboratively models these knowledge sources through physics prototype matching, graph-structured knowledge encoding, historical case retrieval, cross-evidence consistency analysis, and reliability estimation, thereby generating knowledge representations for enhancing temporal features and correcting classification results. Based on this module, KGF-ELM employs a dual-level reliability-aware fusion mechanism. At the feature level, physical residuals and graph-guided knowledge representations are adaptively incorporated into temporal features according to their reliability. At the decision level, reliability gating, minority-class protection, and bounded knowledge correction are used to safely refine the classification results and reduce the negative influence of unreliable knowledge on the base model.

AI.tldr: KGF-ELM is a Knowledge Graph Fusion Network that integrates physical evidence, ELM prototypes, relational knowledge graphs, and historical discharge cases to improve ELM recognition in tokamak plasmas, using a dual-level reliability-aware fusion mechanism.
AI.motivation: Deep time-series models for ELM prediction are purely data-driven, lacking explicit use of ELM physics, plasma operating states, and historical discharge experience, causing confusion between similar temporal patterns, especially under severe class imbalance.
AI.method: A Knowledge Graph Collaborative Fusion Module (KGCFM) organizes multi-source knowledge (current time window physical evidence, ELM prototypes, relational knowledge graph representations, similar historical cases) via physics prototype matching, graph-structured knowledge encoding, historical case retrieval, cross-evidence consistency analysis, and reliability estimation. A dual-level reliability-aware fusion mechanism then adaptively incorporates knowledge at the feature level and refines decisions via reliability gating, minority-class protection, and bounded knowledge correction.
AI.result: The abstract reports that KGCFM generates knowledge representations to enhance temporal features and correct classification results, with the dual-level fusion safely refining outputs and reducing the negative influence of unreliable knowledge on the base model.
AI.conclusion: KGF-ELM addresses the limitations of data-driven ELM prediction by integrating physics and historical knowledge through a reliability-aware fusion framework, improving recognition robustness particularly under class imbalance.

title: Global Strong Solutions for the Affine Darken Class of Maxwell-Stefan Diffusion Systems
summary: The core-diagonal closure of Bothe and Druet identifies multicomponent Darken diffusion as a thermodynamically consistent Maxwell-Stefan model in which the constitutive data are species tracer diffusivities. Building on the Stieltjes-coordinate and De Giorgi regularity framework introduced in our recent preprint for additive Maxwell-Stefan frictions, we prove global maximal-$L^p$ strong well-posedness, without smallness assumptions, for the affine Darken class with composition-dependent scalar coefficients and uniformly positive tracer diffusivities. We show that this is exactly the maximal Darken class preserving the fixed Stieltjes eigenframe underlying the global argument. For general smooth, uniformly positive Darken tracer diffusivities we also derive the direct constrained flux form, exact mixing-entropy symmetrization, Fisher dissipation, composition-uniform normal ellipticity, and local strong well-posedness. Solutions in the affine class remain uniformly separated from the simplex boundary, become classical for positive times, and converge exponentially to equilibrium. Constant multiplicative frictions, including repeated factors, are covered by grouping species with equal factors.

AI.tldr: This paper proves global maximal-$L^p$ strong well-posedness, without smallness assumptions, for the affine Darken multicomponent diffusion class with composition-dependent scalar coefficients, and characterizes it as the maximal Darken class preserving a fixed Stieltjes eigenframe.
AI.motivation: Multicomponent Darken diffusion is identified via the Bothe-Druet core-diagonal closure as a thermodynamically consistent Maxwell-Stefan model with tracer diffusivities as constitutive data. The authors aim to extend their Stieltjes-coordinate and De Giorgi regularity framework—previously developed for additive Maxwell-Stefan frictions—to the multiplicative Darken setting, and to isolate the largest class where the global argument still works.
AI.method: Building on the Stieltjes-coordinate and De Giorgi regularity framework from their preprint, the authors analyze the affine Darken class with composition-dependent scalar coefficients and uniformly positive tracer diffusivities. They show it is exactly the maximal Darken class preserving the fixed Stieltjes eigenframe. For general smooth, uniformly positive Darken tracer diffusivities, they derive the direct constrained flux form, exact mixing-entropy symmetrization, Fisher dissipation, composition-uniform normal ellipticity, and local strong well-posedness. Constant multiplicative frictions with repeated factors are handled by grouping species with equal factors.
AI.result: Global maximal-$L^p$ strong well-posedness is established without smallness assumptions for the affine Darken class. Solutions stay uniformly separated from the simplex boundary, become classical for positive times, and converge exponentially to equilibrium.
AI.conclusion: The affine Darken class is exactly the maximal Darken class for which the fixed-Stieltjes-eigenframe global regularity argument succeeds, and it admits global strong solutions with boundary separation and exponential equilibration; broader Darken classes yield only local well-posedness unless further structure (e.g., grouped equal frictions) is imposed.

title: A higher order lattice-based method for high-dimensional numerical integration using periodization
summary: We present a novel numerical integration method for non-periodic functions over the high-dimensional unit cube $[0,1]^s$ by a specially crafted (unequally-)weighted quadrature rule using transformed lattice points, with the additional option of subsampling. The method is designed for integrands whose mixed derivatives up to order $α$ are square-integrable with respect to a product Chebyshev density. The ingredients are (i) periodizing the integrand, (ii) approximating the smooth periodic function by a kernel interpolant at lattice points, (iii) integrating exactly the product of the kernel interpolant and the nonsmooth density, together with subsampling alternatives for (ii) and~(iii). With $|J|$ corresponding to the number of function evaluations, we achieve the convergence rate close to the order $|J|^{-(α-1/2)}$ and $|J|^{-α}\,($1.110721$)^s$, where the implied constants are independent of $s$ under favorable conditions. We can interpolate these two results to trade between the convergence rate and the growth in $s$. We provide numerical experiments to demonstrate our theory.

AI.tldr: A novel weighted quadrature method for integrating non-periodic functions over the high-dimensional unit cube, using transformed lattice points, periodization, and kernel interpolation, achieving dimension-robust convergence rates with an optional subsampling trade-off.
AI.motivation: Numerical integration of non-periodic functions in high dimensions is challenging due to the curse of dimensionality and loss of smoothness at boundaries. The paper aims for a quadrature rule with convergence rates and constants independent of dimension s under favorable conditions.
AI.method: (i) Periodize the integrand; (ii) approximate the smooth periodic function via a kernel interpolant at (transformed) lattice points; (iii) integrate exactly the product of the kernel interpolant and the nonsmooth density. An unequally-weighted quadrature rule with subsampling alternatives is used for steps (ii) and (iii).
AI.result: With |J| function evaluations, the method achieves convergence rates close to |J|^{-(α-1/2)} and |J|^{-α}(1.110721)^s, where implied constants are independent of s under favorable conditions. The two results can be interpolated to trade off convergence rate against growth in s. Numerical experiments confirm the theory.
AI.conclusion: The proposed weighted-lattice quadrature scheme provides an effective, dimension-robust approach for high-dimensional integration of non-periodic functions, with a tunable balance between convergence rate and dimensional dependence, validated numerically.

title: An S-matrix Formalism for the Nonclassical Optical Response of Plasmonic Nanowires
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: This paper reports a computational scheme which predicts the light-matter interaction in multiple mesoscopic plasmonic nanowires (NWs), each of which includes concentric or eccentric constituent wires. Lying at the core of the proposed scheme is the S-Matrix of each individual cylindrical interface. The optical response of the materials inside and outside each interface can be described by three popular mesoscopic models: the Hydrodynamic Drude model (HDM) and its diffusive variant, namely the Generalized Nonlocal Optical Response (GNOR) model, as well as the Surface Response Model (SRM). To take into account the relative displacements between the cylindrical interfaces, the addition theorem is applied to construct the main equation behind the algorithm, where the possibility of longitudinal waves intrinsic in the HDM and GNOR models is also included. The optical responses calculated by the proposed S Matrix Method are compared with an in-house developed boundary element method (BEM) toolbox for a single gold NW and an eccentric dual-material NW, and excellent agreements are seen. The algorithm is further physically checked for a sodium nanolens trimer featuring large field focusing, and the effects of the HDM and the SRM are compared.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational S-Matrix Method to predict light-matter interaction in multiple mesoscopic plasmonic nanowires with concentric or eccentric cylindrical interfaces, accounting for nonlocal optical responses via HDM, GNOR, and SRM.
AI.motivation: Mesoscopic plasmonic nanowires exhibit complex optical responses that require accurate modeling of nonlocal effects and multiple interacting cylindrical interfaces, which existing methods may not handle efficiently together.
AI.method: Uses the S-Matrix of each individual cylindrical interface as the core, combining HDM, GNOR, and SRM to describe optical responses. The addition theorem handles relative displacements between interfaces, incorporating longitudinal waves intrinsic to HDM and GNOR.
AI.result: Optical responses from the proposed S-Matrix Method show excellent agreement with an in-house boundary element method (BEM) toolbox for a single gold nanowire and an eccentric dual-material nanowire. The algorithm is further validated on a sodium nanolens trimer exhibiting large field focusing, with HDM and SRM effects compared.
AI.conclusion: The S-Matrix Method is a reliable and versatile tool for modeling mesoscopic plasmonic nanowires, correctly capturing nonlocal and geometric complexity, as verified against BEM and applied to a nanolens trimer.

title: Rapid Vacuum Response Calculations for Non-axisymmetric Plasma Geometries
summary: We present a fast, open-source calculation of the vacuum response matrix and surface inductance in non-axisymmetric geometries capable of running with up to 10^5 boundary points in tens of seconds on a laptop. Ideal magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) stability modeling for free boundary modes requires the perturbed vacuum energy. We extend the VACUUM code to non-axisymmetric geometries in the new Julia implementation of the Generalized Perturbed Equilibrium Code, combining a collocation approach to the boundary integral equations with a high-order singularity correction scheme. The correction is recast into explicit quadrature weights acting on the collocation values, which allows the corrected operator to be assembled explicitly rather than applied to a given surface field, and the structure of that matrix under field-period and stellarator symmetry is then exploited to reduce storage and solve cost. We find that the vacuum response matrix converges at fourth order or greater in the grid spacing, reaching a given accuracy on a coarser grid than previous implementations without the high-order method. The non-axisymmetric calculation converges to the axisymmetric VACUUM result for a tokamak and the CAS3D result for a W7-X stellarator equilibrium. This work enables fast free boundary ideal MHD stability and perturbed equilibrium calculations in stellarators.

AI.tldr: A fast, open-source Julia implementation (GPEC) computes the vacuum response matrix and surface inductance for non-axisymmetric geometries, enabling free-boundary ideal MHD stability modeling in stellarators.
AI.motivation: Free-boundary MHD stability modeling requires the perturbed vacuum energy, but existing tools lack a fast method for non-axisymmetric geometries, so this work extends the VACUUM code accordingly.
AI.method: Combines a collocation approach to boundary integral equations with a high-order singularity correction scheme, recast as explicit quadrature weights so the corrected operator is assembled explicitly; exploits field-period and stellarator symmetry to reduce storage and solve cost.
AI.result: Handles up to 10^5 boundary points in tens of seconds on a laptop; vacuum response matrix converges at fourth order or higher in grid spacing, achieving target accuracy on coarser grids than prior implementations; matches VACUUM for a tokamak and CAS3D for a W7-X stellarator.
AI.conclusion: Enables fast free-boundary ideal MHD stability and perturbed equilibrium calculations in stellarators.

title: Banach-Valued Stieltjes Calculus and Linear Parabolic Evolution Equations with Posterior States
summary:
We develop a Banach-valued lateral Stieltjes calculus adapted to linear evolution equations on a Gelfand triple \[
  V\hookrightarrow H\simeq H^*\hookrightarrow V^*. \] The evolution problem is formulated with the posterior state, \[
  D_g u(t)+A(t) S_g u(t)=f(t),\qquad u(a)=u_0. \] This choice is decisive at atoms of the Stieltjes measure: if $δ=Δ_g(r)>0$, the equation yields the implicit variational resolvent \[
  (I+δA(r))u(r^+)=u(r)+δf(r). \] We prove a Banach-valued lateral product formula, a weak--strong reconstruction theorem, and a Stieltjes analogue of the Lions--Magenes energy identity. In the separable Hilbert setting considered here, the stable projection chain used in the proof is shown to exist automatically by a spectral-band construction. The latter contains the exact positive jump contribution \[
  \frac12\sum_r\|u(r^+)-u(r)\|_H^2. \] Existence is constructed independently by Galerkin approximation and by a Rothe scheme adapted to the Stieltjes mass and its atoms. The Rothe construction does not use spatial projections. We also explain why the available Aubin--Lions theorem for anterior Stieltjes--Bochner evolution graphs is not automatically applicable to the posterior energy space and, in the present linear coercive setting, is not needed. A heat equation with Stieltjes time is included as a model application. The claims are positioned relative to earlier Stieltjes parabolic equations, general measure-driven evolution, and operator-valued-measure parabolic systems; no priority is claimed for measure-driven parabolic theory or Galerkin approximation in general.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a Banach-valued lateral Stieltjes calculus for linear evolution equations on a Gelfand triple, formulated with the posterior state, proving a lateral product formula, weak--strong reconstruction theorem, and a Stieltjes Lions--Magenes energy identity, with existence via Galerkin and Rothe schemes.
AI.motivation: Evolution problems driven by Stieltjes measures with atoms require a calculus that handles the posterior (post-jump) state correctly, since anterior formulations fail at atoms of the measure. A Banach-valued framework on a Gelfand triple is needed to treat such measure-driven parabolic equations rigorously.
AI.method: A Banach-valued lateral Stieltjes calculus is built on a Gelfand triple V↪H≃H*↪V*, using the posterior state formulation D_g u + A(t)S_g u = f with an implicit variational resolvent (I+δA(r))u(r+)=u(r)+δf(r) at atoms. The analysis proves a lateral product formula, weak--strong reconstruction, and a Stieltjes energy identity; the stable projection chain is obtained by a spectral-band construction. Existence is derived independently via Galerkin approximation and a spatially projection-free Rothe scheme.
AI.result: The claims are proved: the lateral product formula, weak--strong reconstruction theorem, and Stieltjes analogue of the Lions--Magenes energy identity, whose energy contains the exact positive jump term (1/2)Σ_r ||u(r+)-u(r)||_H^2. The stable projection chain is shown to exist automatically in the separable Hilbert setting. Aubin--Lions is shown not to be automatically applicable to the posterior energy space and, in the linear coercive case, not needed. A Stieltjes-time heat equation is given as a model application.
AI.conclusion: The posterior-state Stieltjes calculus provides a self-contained framework for linear measure-driven evolution, with existence independent of spatial projections and no reliance on Aubin--Lions in this coercive setting. The work is positioned relative to earlier Stieltjes parabolic, measure-driven evolution, and operator-valued-measure parabolic systems, with no priority claimed for measure-driven parabolic theory or Galerkin approximation generally.

title: Sign-Switched Antithetic Coupling for Signed Gradient-Particle Methods
comment: 46 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23055907
summary: Gradient random-walk methods represent the spatial derivative of a solution by signed particles and recover the solution by summing their masses. We reduce the sampling error of such simulations for one-dimensional convection-diffusion equations by running them in pairs with particles matched in order of position. Reflected pairing, the standard antithetic choice, gives matched particles opposite displacements. In sign-switched pairing, matched particles of equal sign receive opposite displacements and those of opposite sign the same displacement. Each simulation keeps the probability distribution of the solver, so the pair average has the expectation and bias of one simulation. For a fixed matching, we prove that sign-switched pairing minimizes the variance contribution of each matched pair at the last diffusion step. We also derive an exact formula for the variance it removes relative to reflected pairing. For the heat equation both results extend to every step, and we measure the accumulated variance reduction numerically. In Burgers tests, with sample sizes chosen from pilot runs and checked on fresh runs, sign-switched pairing meets a mean-squared-error target with 4 simulations, compared with 65 for independent sampling and 34 for reflected pairing. Against within-sign pairing, which matches only particles of equal sign, it has about 26% lower variance with 8192 particles. With 2048 particles it meets a second target in about 40% less time. The gain persists for further profiles, later times, other viscosities, and a cubic flux, supporting sign-switched pairing as an inexpensive way to improve repeated field estimates where particles of opposite sign meet.

AI.tldr: Introduces "sign-switched pairing," a particle-matching scheme that reduces sampling variance in gradient random-walk simulations of 1D convection-diffusion equations by pairing particles with matched positions, achieving large MSE improvements in Burgers tests.
AI.motivation: Gradient random-walk methods suffer from sampling error. Reducing this error cheaply (without adding simulations or particles) would improve repeated field estimates, especially where particles of opposite sign meet.
AI.method: Run simulations in pairs with particles matched by position. Compare schemes: reflected (standard antithetic, opposite displacements), sign-switched (equal-sign pairs get opposite displacements, opposite-sign pairs get same displacement), and within-sign. Prove sign-switched minimizes per-pair variance contribution at the last diffusion step for a fixed matching, and derive an exact formula for variance removed vs. reflected pairing; extend to all steps for the heat equation. Validate on Burgers tests with pilot-run sample sizes.
AI.result: Sign-switched pairing meets an MSE target with 4 simulations vs. 65 (independent) and 34 (reflected). It has ~26% lower variance than within-sign pairing at 8192 particles, and meets a second target in ~40% less time at 2048 particles. Gains persist across profiles, later times, other viscosities, and a cubic flux.
AI.conclusion: Sign-switched pairing is an inexpensive way to improve repeated field estimates in gradient random-walk simulations, particularly where particles of opposite sign meet.

title: RFBniCS: An open-source simulation framework for redox flow batteries
summary: We present RFBniCS, an open-source finite-element framework implemented in FEniCSx for simulating redox-flow-battery (RFB) half-cells. RFBniCS solves an established macro-homogeneous porous-electrode model accounting for strongly coupled electrolyte flow, multicomponent species transport, ionic and electronic charge conservation, and interfacial Faradaic charge transfer. Different from other open-access tools, RFBniCS can perform transient RFB half-cell simulations in one-, two-, and three-dimensional geometries while explicitly resolving the transport of both redox-active and supporting-electrolyte species. It also describes electrolyte flow through porous electrodes and, in the three-dimensional formulation, through adjacent flow channels. To verify the implementation, RFBniCS's predictions in parameter-limiting regimes are compared against other published implementations, with RFBniCS generally showing superior accuracy and speed. We further demonstrate RFBniCS's capabilities by a simulation of the transient response of the negative half-cell of a vanadium redox flow battery, with a moderately concentrated supporting electrolyte. In the current implementation, RFBniCS provides the computational basis for studying redox-flow-battery half-cells and can be extended to complex flow-field designs, alternative chemistries, full-cell coupling, detailed membrane transport, and additional multiphysics effects.

AI.tldr: RFBniCS is an open-source FEniCSx finite-element framework for transient 1D/2D/3D redox-flow-battery half-cell simulations, coupling porous-electrode flow, multicomponent transport, charge conservation, and Faradaic transfer, with verification and a vanadium battery demo.
AI.motivation: Existing open-access RFB tools often lack transient, multidimensional half-cell simulation with explicit resolution of both redox-active and supporting-electrolyte species. RFBniCS is introduced to fill this gap as a computational basis for studying RFB half-cells.
AI.method: Implemented in FEniCSx, RFBniCS solves a macro-homogeneous porous-electrode model with strongly coupled electrolyte flow, multicomponent species transport, ionic/electronic charge conservation, and interfacial Faradaic charge transfer. It supports 1D, 2D, and 3D geometries, resolves redox-active and supporting species, and models flow through porous electrodes and (in 3D) adjacent channels.
AI.result: In parameter-limiting regimes, RFBniCS predictions agree with published implementations while generally showing superior accuracy and speed. A transient simulation of a vanadium RFB negative half-cell with moderately concentrated supporting electrolyte demonstrates its capabilities.
AI.conclusion: RFBniCS provides a computational foundation for RFB half-cell studies and is extensible to complex flow-field designs, alternative chemistries, full-cell coupling, detailed membrane transport, and other multiphysics effects.

title: Normal-Field Evolution and the Breakdown of Classical Tearing in Current Sheets
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to Physical Review E
summary: Classical resistive tearing theory assumes a prescribed current-sheet equilibrium, but a finite normal magnetic field can evolve the background on the tearing timescale. For a transversely pressure-balanced Harris profile of initial half-thickness $a$ and asymptotic reconnecting-field magnitude $B_0$, threaded by uniform $B_n$ ($ξ=B_n/B_0$), we derive an exact evolution in ideal magnetohydrodynamics: counter-propagating Alfvenic fronts broaden the neutral layer and generate a central sheet-parallel flow with shear at its flanks. Inner-layer estimates recover $ξ_{\mathrm{crit}}\sim S^{-3/4}$ for breakdown of the classical resistive balance, where $S$ is the Lundquist number based on $a$. Numerical frozen-profile calculations show loss of central resistive dominance and decreasing tearing growth as the neutral layer expands. Eigenfunction comparisons at fixed wavenumber and predominantly Doppler-shifted propagation support a normal-field-modified continuation of classical tearing. The normal field supplies no net perturbation energy. Energy extraction from the reconnecting-field gradient weakens as the sheet broadens. The velocity-gradient contribution becomes comparable when the neutral-layer width approaches the initial sheet thickness, without reversing the decline in growth. For $S=10^6$, $\mathrm{Pr}_m=0$, and $ξ=10^{-4}$, the maximum growth rate falls by a factor of about ten from its initial value at neutral-layer half-width $w\simeq1.59a$, where the growth and broadening times become equal. Only about 0.18 additional upper-envelope e-folds are estimated between this crossing and $w/a=2$, where the growth rate is about 25 times smaller than its initial value. These results support dynamical suppression of further linear amplification over the sampled evolution, even though the instantaneous spectrum remains unstable.

AI.tldr: A uniform normal magnetic field dynamically evolves a Harris current sheet on tearing timescales, broadening the neutral layer via Alfvénic fronts and suppressing resistive tearing growth.
AI.motivation: Classical resistive tearing theory assumes a fixed current-sheet equilibrium, ignoring that a finite normal magnetic field can evolve the background over the tearing timescale, so the standard resistive balance may break down.
AI.method: For a transversely pressure-balanced Harris profile (half-thickness a, reconnecting field B0) threaded by uniform Bn (ξ = Bn/B0), an exact ideal-MHD evolution is derived. Inner-layer estimates and numerical frozen-profile calculations are used.
AI.result: Counter-propagating Alfvénic fronts broaden the neutral layer and create a central sheet-parallel shear flow. The classical resistive balance breaks down at ξ_crit ~ S^(-3/4). Growth rate decreases as the layer expands; for S=10^6, Pr_m=0, ξ=10^-4, the maximum growth rate drops ~10x at w≈1.59a, with only ~0.18 additional e-folds up to w/a=2 (growth ~25x smaller).
AI.conclusion: The normal field supplies no net perturbation energy; energy extraction from the reconnecting-field gradient weakens as the sheet broadens. Comparison supports a normal-field-modified continuation of classical tearing, but the dynamics suppress further linear amplification—dynamical suppression despite an instantaneously unstable spectrum.

title: Logarithmic concentration for the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation on the two-dimensional torus
summary: We construct a smooth solution of the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a square two-dimensional torus which is global in both time directions and concentrates at one point as time tends to positive infinity. Its mass is the mass of the Euclidean ground state and its energy is zero. If $λ(t)$ denotes its concentration scale and $L$ the period, then $L/λ(t)=2\log t+\frac{11}{2}\log\log t+O(1)$. The solution approaches a phased, periodized ground state with an error tending to zero in every fixed Sobolev space. In particular, its $H^s$ norm is asymptotic to an explicit constant times $(\log t)^s$ for every $s>0$. We also prove uniqueness, up to constant phase and time translation, within the quantitative single-profile asymptotic class used in the construction. The mechanism is the exponentially small interaction of the profile with its periodic images. Exact mass and energy constraints select the concentrating branch, while a positive energy on the moving constrained space controls the terminal-value problem at every fixed regularity order.

AI.tldr: Construction of a global (both time directions) smooth solution to the focusing cubic NLS on a 2D square torus that concentrates at one point as t→+∞, with mass equal to the Euclidean ground state mass and zero energy, and a logarithmic concentration law.
AI.motivation: To exhibit and characterize a concentrating (blow-up-type, but global and forward-in-time) singular solution for focusing cubic NLS on a torus, where periodic images and interaction effects are key. Such a solution clarifies the dynamics of concentration and the role of mass/energy constraints on a compact domain.
AI.method: Constructs a single-profile asymptotic solution via the exponentially small interaction between the concentrating profile and its periodic images. Uses exact mass and energy constraints to select a concentrating branch, and a positive energy on the moving constrained space to control the terminal-value problem at each fixed regularity order. Proves uniqueness up to constant phase and time translation within the quantitative single-profile asymptotic class.
AI.result: Obtains a smooth solution global in both time directions concentrating at one point as t→+∞, with mass of the Euclidean ground state and zero energy. Concentration scale satisfies L/λ(t)=2log t+(11/2)loglog t+O(1). The solution approaches a phased, periodized ground state with error tending to zero in every fixed Sobolev space; its H^s norm is asymptotic to an explicit constant times (log t)^s for every s>0. Uniqueness proven within the asymptotic class.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism is the exponentially small interaction of the profile with its periodic images. Exact mass and energy constraints select the concentrating branch, and positive energy on the moving constrained space controls the terminal-value problem. This yields a unique (up to phase and time translation) quantitative single-profile concentrating solution.

title: Dirichlet--Neumann waveform relaxation for heterogeneous heat equations: fully discrete $l^2$ analysis
summary:
We consider two coupled linear heat equations on different spatial domains that interact through a lower dimensional interface. This models conjugate heat transfer. The problem is solved using Dirichlet--Neumann waveform relaxation. This allows the subproblems to be solved using separate codes, a so called partitioned approach. Our overall goal is to develop more efficient partitioned methods, and to this end, we want reliable error estimates.
  Here, we use an exponentially weighted Fourier technique to derive new error estimates in $l^2$ for finite time $T$ in the fully discrete setting. These describe both linear and superlinear behavior. We show that the fully discrete estimate is close to a previously obtained time discrete estimate and independent of $Δx_1$ and $Δx_2$ when the CFL number in the subsolvers is large. We also show that the convergence behaviour depends on the ratio $Δx_1/Δx_2$ when the CFL number is small.
  Our numerical experiments show that the fully discrete estimate is accurate across a wide range of grid sizes $Δx_1, Δx_2$, time step sizes $Δt$ and $T$.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a Dirichlet–Neumann waveform relaxation method for two coupled linear heat equations on different domains interacting through a lower-dimensional interface (conjugate heat transfer), deriving new fully discrete l² error estimates via an exponentially weighted Fourier technique.
AI.motivation: To develop more efficient partitioned methods for conjugate heat transfer, reliable error estimates are needed. Existing time-discrete estimates are insufficient because practical implementations are fully discrete.
AI.method: A partitioned Dirichlet–Neumann waveform relaxation approach enables subproblems to be solved with separate codes. An exponentially weighted Fourier technique is used to derive new error estimates in l² for finite time T in the fully discrete setting, capturing both linear and superlinear convergence.
AI.result: The fully discrete estimate is close to the earlier time-discrete estimate and independent of Δx1 and Δx2 when the CFL number in the subsolvers is large. When the CFL number is small, the convergence behavior depends on the ratio Δx1/Δx2. Numerical experiments confirm accuracy across a wide range of grid sizes, time steps, and T.
AI.conclusion: Fully discrete error estimates for Dirichlet–Neumann waveform relaxation in conjugate heat transfer are established and validated, revealing CFL-dependent and mesh-ratio-dependent convergence behavior.

title: Loading history and window geometry bound compact-state slip ranking during granular shear startup
summary: Granular slip forecasting can conflate material state, loading progress, and the geometry of event-centered sampling. We separated these contributions in slowly sheared two-dimensional frictional disks using a compact neural score of stress, pressure, coordination, non-affine motion, and force-network observables. The model was developed on 36 trajectories and frozen efore testing on 18 new trajectories under two nested stress-drop definitions. Inspection of held-out results revealed post-event sampling asymmetry; recovery-aware analyses are therefore descriptive. With trajectories weighted equally, the compact score ranked near-slip windows above both prevalence and within-trajectory circular-phase controls under both definitions (representative average precision 0.310 versus prevalence 0.173; phase-null upper bound 0.257). Loading-history coordinates ranked more strongly, reaching 0.534 for causal elapsed strain. The recovery-aware rule retained 78.4\% of activity-gated events and preferentially selected longer preceding intervals; ranking by time since the previous catalogued event remained compatible with a count-conditioned geometry null. Compact observables thus contain temporally aligned slip information, but stronger loading-history baselines and window-geometry sensitivity bound that evidence. These startup data do not isolate a state-specific short-horizon precursor beyond loading history or support a renewal interpretation of elapsed-strain ranking.

AI.tldr: A compact neural score separates slip-related signals from loading-history and sampling-geometry effects in sheared 2D frictional disks, showing only bounded pre-slip information that remains confounded by loading history.
AI.motivation: Granular slip forecasting often conflates material state, loading progress, and the geometry of event-centered sampling, making it unclear whether observed signals reflect true precursors or artifacts.
AI.method: Slowly sheared two-dimensional frictional disks modeled with a compact neural score of stress, pressure, coordination, non-affine motion, and force-network observables. Developed on 36 trajectories and frozen before testing on 18 new trajectories under two nested stress-drop definitions, with recovery-aware and circular-phase controls.
AI.result: The compact score ranked near-slip windows above prevalence and phase-null controls under both definitions (average precision 0.310 vs. 0.173 prevalence; phase-null 0.257). Loading-history coordinates ranked more strongly, reaching 0.534 for causal elapsed strain; the recovery-aware rule retained 78.4% of activity-gated events, and time-since-last-event ranking was compatible with a geometry null.
AI.conclusion: Compact observables contain temporally aligned slip information, but stronger loading-history baselines and window-geometry sensitivity bound this evidence. The data do not isolate a state-specific short-horizon precursor beyond loading history nor support a renewal interpretation of elapsed-strain ranking.

title: Is Your AI Fast Enough to Run a Fusion Reactor?
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly used in feedback control loops for nuclear fusion, where inference speed and predictable timing are critical. We summarize lessons from models deployed for control on the DIII-D tokamak and develop a benchmark to compare inference backends across ten neural networks and model components from fusion control and diagnostic pipelines. For models greater than five million parameters, the CPU backends take tens to thousands of milliseconds, while GPU inference is substantially faster, suggesting an upper limit on CPU-oriented development for control. These results show why the deployment backend must be selected together with the model and its control-cycle budget.

AI.tldr: Lessons from deploying ML models for control on the DIII-D tokamak, plus a benchmark comparing inference backends (CPU vs GPU) across ten neural networks from fusion control and diagnostic pipelines.
AI.motivation: ML models are increasingly used in feedback control loops for nuclear fusion, where inference speed and predictable timing are critical.
AI.method: Summarized deployment lessons from models used for control on DIII-D and developed a benchmark comparing inference backends across ten neural networks and model components from fusion control and diagnostic pipelines.
AI.result: For models larger than five million parameters, CPU backends take tens to thousands of milliseconds, while GPU inference is substantially faster—suggesting an upper limit on CPU-oriented development for control.
AI.conclusion: The deployment backend must be selected together with the model and its control-cycle budget.

title: Global Well-Posedness of the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky Equation in One and Two Dimensions under a Codimension-One Constraint
summary: We study the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equation in one, two, and three spatial dimensions subject to a codimension-one constraint. The constraint preserves the \(L^2\)-norm of the solution and consequently provides a uniform a priori bound that plays a central role in the higher-order energy estimates. In one spatial dimension, we establish global well-posedness by means of a Fourier--Galerkin approximation and compactness arguments. In two and three dimensions, we first prove the existence and uniqueness of local strong solutions using analytic semigroup theory and the Banach fixed-point theorem. In two dimensions, the preserved \(L^2\)-norm, combined with the Agmon inequality and suitable higher-order energy estimates, allows us to control the nonlinear terms and obtain global-in-time a priori bounds. Consequently, we establish the existence and uniqueness of global strong solutions for arbitrary sufficiently regular initial data, without any smallness assumption. This provides a global well-posedness result for the constrained two-dimensional KS equation, in contrast with the corresponding unconstrained problem, for which global well-posedness of strong solutions remains open in general. In three dimensions, although the constraint yields a uniform \(L^2\)-bound, the available interpolation and Agmon estimates are insufficient to close the higher-order energy estimate. This identifies a genuine dimension-dependent obstruction to extending the global regularity argument to three dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation under a codimension-one constraint preserving the L²-norm, proving global well-posedness in 1D and 2D but identifying a genuine obstruction in 3D.
AI.motivation: For the unconstrained KS equation, global well-posedness of strong solutions remains open in general. The authors introduce a codimension-one constraint that preserves the L²-norm, providing a uniform a priori bound to enable higher-order energy estimates and possibly global regularity.
AI.method: The constrained KS equation is analyzed in 1D, 2D, and 3D. In 1D, global well-posedness is shown via Fourier–Galerkin approximation and compactness. In 2D and 3D, local strong solutions are obtained using analytic semigroup theory and the Banach fixed-point theorem. In 2D, the preserved L²-norm with Agmon inequality and higher-order energy estimates controls nonlinear terms.
AI.result: In 1D, global well-posedness is established. In 2D, global strong solutions exist and are unique for arbitrary sufficiently regular initial data without smallness assumptions. In 3D, despite a uniform L²-bound, existing interpolation and Agmon estimates are insufficient to close the higher-order energy estimate.
AI.conclusion: The constraint yields global well-posedness for the 2D constrained KS equation, contrasting with the unconstrained problem's open status. In 3D, a genuine dimension-dependent obstruction prevents extending the global regularity argument.

title: Finite element exterior calculus for spectra and pseudospectra of advection-diffusion of differential forms
summary: Numerical investigations of dynamo action have remained active in fluid mechanics over the past decades, presenting numerous challenges and open problems. Meanwhile, the development of structure-preserving methods and finite element exterior calculus (FEEC) inspires a revisit of numerical dynamo studies and an exploration of existing open questions in computation. In this paper, we present a FEEC approach for dynamo problems. In particular, we investigate structure-preserving finite element schemes for computing the spectra and pseudospectra of advection-diffusion operators of differential forms. The schemes and their analysis are based on finite element de Rham complexes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a structure-preserving finite element exterior calculus (FEEC) approach for dynamo problems, specifically for computing spectra and pseudospectra of advection-diffusion operators acting on differential forms, based on finite element de Rham complexes.
AI.motivation: Numerical dynamo studies remain challenging with open problems, while advances in structure-preserving methods and FEEC motivate revisiting these studies and exploring open computational questions.
AI.method: A FEEC approach using structure-preserving finite element schemes built on finite element de Rham complexes, applied to advection-diffusion operators of differential forms for spectral and pseudospectral computation.
AI.result: The paper develops and analyzes structure-preserving finite element schemes for computing spectra and pseudospectra of advection-diffusion operators of differential forms.
AI.conclusion: FEEC provides a promising framework for numerical dynamo investigations, enabling structure-preserving computation relevant to open questions in the field.

title: Electromagnetic drift-kinetic particle-in-cell model with energy and charge conservation for studying finite-$β$ plasmas
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to Journal of Computational Physics
summary: The paper proposes a generalization of the fully implicit energy- and charge-conserving electromagnetic particle-in-cell method to the case where the lightest type of plasma particle (electrons) is described in the drift-kinetic approximation. This allows us to remove the very strict time step limitation of this method requiring to resolve the gyrorotation of electrons. Since the drift-kinetic model is only applicable to light particles whose contribution to plasma polarization is small, this model can be further simplified by neglecting the electron polarization drift and including in Maxwell's equations, in addition to the current of gyrocenters, only the magnetization current. In order for such a hybrid model to retain conservative properties in finite-difference form, a method of self-consistent interpolation of $\nabla B$ in the mirror force from grid to particle and the magnetization vector from particle to grid is proposed. Unlike existing drift-kinetic models, this model is not limited to considering small perturbations near a given equilibrium, and therefore allows one to study the formation of plasma equilibria in regimes with a finite ratio of plasma to magnetic field pressure. Testing of the parallel code implemented in C++ using the PETSc library confirmed the fulfillment of the finite-difference laws of energy and charge conservation, as well as the ability of the model (in the drift-kinetic version for all types of particles) to correctly reproduce the diamagnetic effect and longitudinal ion-acoustic wave.

AI.tldr: A fully implicit, energy- and charge-conserving hybrid PIC method is generalized to treat electrons via drift-kinetic approximation, removing the strict time-step limit of resolving electron gyrorotation while preserving conservation laws.
AI.motivation: The original fully implicit energy- and charge-conserving electromagnetic PIC method requires resolving electron gyrorotation, imposing a very strict time-step limitation. A drift-kinetic treatment of light particles could relax this, but must retain the method's conservative properties.
AI.method: Electrons are described in the drift-kinetic approximation. The model neglects electron polarization drift and includes only the gyrocenter current and magnetization current in Maxwell's equations. A self-consistent interpolation scheme for nabla-B in the mirror force (grid to particle) and the magnetization vector (particle to grid) preserves finite-difference conservation.
AI.result: Testing of the parallel C++/PETSc code confirmed satisfaction of finite-difference energy and charge conservation laws, and correct reproduction of the diamagnetic effect and the longitudinal ion-acoustic wave (in the drift-kinetic version for all particle types).
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid drift-kinetic PIC model removes the electron gyrorotation time-step restriction, retains conservative finite-difference properties, and is not limited to small perturbations near equilibrium, enabling study of plasma equilibria at finite plasma-to-magnetic pressure ratios.

title: Transport Impacts of Resonant Island Chains in Fusion Plasmas
summary: Magnetic field-line transport in magnetically confined plasmas is commonly modeled as diffusion through stochastic magnetic layers generated by resonant perturbations. However, experimentally relevant magnetic configurations frequently exhibit transport rates that are substantially slower than predicted by fully stochastic models, indicating the presence of unresolved dynamical barriers. In this work, we investigate the role of nested resonant island chains and their associated invariant manifolds in regulating transport within the edge magnetic topology of DIII-D tokamak discharge #171491 subjected to strong n=3 resonant magnetic perturbations. Using field-line tracing, Poincare analysis, and manifold calculations, we identify a hierarchy of homoclinic and heteroclinic tangles associated with both period-one and period-ten hyperbolic points. A systematic construction based on primary intersection points is developed to extract partial transport barriers from the full manifold geometry and divide the chaotic region into dynamically distinct domains. Monte Carlo simulations reveal that field-line escape exhibits a bi-exponential character when only the outermost period-one boundary is considered, reflecting the presence of a long-lived "sticky" region associated with the period-ten island chain. When the inner period-ten boundary is explicitly incorporated into the Monte Carlo, the escape process becomes approximately single exponential and is accurately described by turnstile lobe transport. The measured escape rate agrees with predictions obtained from the turnstile lobe area and the symplectic structure of the field-line map. These results demonstrate that nested tangles provide a quantitative transport skeleton governing magnetic-field-line escape and establish a framework for analyzing transport barriers, cantori, and lobe dynamics in realistic fusion-plasma magnetic configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that nested resonant island tangles create partial transport barriers that regulate field-line escape in a DIII-D RMP discharge, explaining slower-than-stochastic transport.
AI.motivation: Experimentally observed field-line transport rates in magnetically confined plasmas are often slower than fully stochastic models predict, indicating unresolved dynamical barriers. The role of nested resonant island chains and their invariant manifolds in regulating transport is not well understood.
AI.method: Field-line tracing, Poincare analysis, and manifold calculations are applied to the edge magnetic topology of DIII-D discharge #171491 under strong n=3 resonant magnetic perturbations. A systematic construction based on primary intersection points extracts partial transport barriers from full manifold geometry. Monte Carlo simulations and turnstile lobe analysis quantify escape rates.
AI.result: A hierarchy of homoclinic and heteroclinic tangles for period-one and period-ten hyperbolic points is identified. Escape shows bi-exponential behavior when only the outermost period-one boundary is considered, due to a long-lived sticky region linked to the period-ten island chain. Including the inner period-ten boundary yields approximately single-exponential escape accurately described by turnstile lobe transport, with escape rate matching predictions from lobe area and the symplectic map structure.
AI.conclusion: Nested tangles provide a quantitative transport skeleton governing magnetic-field-line escape, offering a framework for analyzing transport barriers, cantori, and lobe dynamics in realistic fusion-plasma configurations.

title: Optimal Control of 2D Navier--Stokes Equations with Constraints of Finite Codimension
summary: We study an optimal control problem for the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations projected onto the tangent space of the $\mathbb{H}$-unit sphere manifold $\mathcal{M} := \{\boldsymbol{u} \in \mathbb{H} : \|\boldsymbol{u}\|_{\mathbb{H}}=1\}$. This geometric projection yields a constrained evolution system of finite codimension, ensuring that the state remains on $\mathcal{M}$ for all times. Using a Faedo-Galerkin approximation technique, we establish the global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to the constrained Navier-Stokes equations with external controls $\boldsymbol{U} \in \mathrm{L}^2(0,T;\mathbb{H})$, together with uniform energy estimates. The associated optimal control problem, minimizing a quadratic cost functional subject to the manifold constraint, is shown to admit at least one optimal pair $(\boldsymbol{u}^*,\boldsymbol{U}^*)$. We derive the first-order necessary optimality conditions by formulating an optimal control system whose state-control pair $(\boldsymbol{u}^*,\boldsymbol{U}^*)$ evolves on the tangent bundle $T\mathcal{M}$ of the constraint manifold $\mathcal{M}$.
