In this setting, the control satisfies $\boldsymbol{U}^*(t)\in T_{\boldsymbol{u}^*(t)}\mathcal{M}$ for all $t\in[0,T]$, ensuring that the dynamics remain confined to the tangent bundle $T\mathcal{M}$. Furthermore, we establish the Fréchet differentiability of the control-to-state mapping $\boldsymbol{U}\mapsto \boldsymbol{u}_{\boldsymbol{U}}$ in $\mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathbb{H})\cap\mathrm{L}^2(0,T;\mathbb{V})$, with the corresponding linearized state characterized as the unique weak solution of a linearized constrained Navier-Stokes system preserving the tangency condition. These results provide a rigorous analytical foundation for the optimal control of fluid flows constrained to nonlinear manifolds.

AI.tldr: The paper studies optimal control of 2D Navier-Stokes equations constrained to the unit sphere manifold, establishing global well-posedness, existence of optimal pairs, first-order optimality conditions on the tangent bundle, and Fréchet differentiability of the control-to-state map.
AI.motivation: Optimal control of fluid flows constrained to nonlinear manifolds lacks a rigorous analytical foundation. The authors aim to provide one for Navier-Stokes dynamics confined to the H-unit sphere manifold.
AI.method: They project the 2D Navier-Stokes equations onto the tangent space of the sphere manifold, producing a finite-codimension constrained evolution system. Using Faedo-Galerkin approximation, they prove global existence, uniqueness, and uniform energy estimates for strong solutions. Optimality conditions are derived via an optimal control system evolving on the tangent bundle TM.
AI.result: Global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions with controls in L^2(0,T;H) are established. The quadratic-cost optimal control problem admits at least one optimal pair. First-order necessary optimality conditions are derived with controls in the tangent space, and the control-to-state map is shown to be Frechet differentiable in C([0,T];H) ∩ L^2(0,T;V), with linearized state as unique weak solution.
AI.conclusion: The results give a rigorous analytical foundation for optimal control of fluid flows constrained to nonlinear manifolds.

title: An Unfitted Hybrid High-Order Method for the Elastodynamics Problem with Imperfect Interface
summary: We design and analyse an unfitted hybrid high-order (HHO) method for the elastic wave equation in a medium made of two components separated by an imperfect interface of linear slip type, across which the traction is continuous and the displacement jump is proportional to the traction through a compliancy tensor $\bK=α\bI+(β-α)\bn\otimes\bn$. The mesh is not fitted to the interface: the discrete unknowns are doubled in the cut cells, the small cuts are cured by a cell agglomeration procedure, and no unknown is attached to the interface. The two specific ingredients of the method are a local symmetric strain reconstruction in each cut subcell, which incorporates the interface condition through the regularised interface stiffness $\bS_h=(h_Tδ^{-1}\bI+\bK)^{-1}$ in the spirit of Hansbo and Hansbo {\em{A finite element method for the simulation of strong and weak discontinuities in solid mechanics.}} {Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Engrg.}, 193, 2004, and an interface stabilisation built from the same matrix. For the space semi-discrete problem we prove that the discrete bilinear form is coercive and continuous, and we derive an energy-error estimate of order $h^{k+1}$ and an $L^2$-error estimate of order $h^{k+2}$, with constants independent of the compliancy parameters and of how the interface cuts the mesh. The scheme is combined either with the Newmark scheme, which conserves a discrete energy exactly, or with singly diagonally implicit Runge--Kutta schemes of order up to four. Numerical experiments in two dimensions confirm the predicted convergence rates for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$, the robustness with respect to the compliancy over sixteen orders of magnitude, and illustrate the propagation of elastic waves across an unresolved slipping interface.

AI.tldr: An unfitted Hybrid High-Order (HHO) method is designed and analyzed for elastic waves across an imperfect (linear slip) interface, with energy-error order h^{k+1} and L²-error order h^{k+2}, robust to compliancy and mesh-interface cuts.
AI.motivation: Standard fitted meshes are cumbersome for problems where an imperfect interface cuts through the domain arbitrarily. A method is needed that avoids interface-conforming meshes while accurately capturing linear slip interface conditions, with error bounds independent of compliancy parameters and how the interface cuts the mesh.
AI.method: Unfitted HHO method: doubled unknowns in cut cells, cell agglomeration to cure small cuts, no unknown on the interface. Key ingredients are (i) a local symmetric strain reconstruction in each cut subcell incorporating the interface condition via the regularized interface stiffness S_h=(h_T δ^{-1} I+K)^{-1}, following Hansbo & Hansbo, and (ii) an interface stabilization built from the same matrix. Time integration via Newmark (exact discrete energy conservation) or SDIRK schemes up to order four.
AI.result: For the space semi-discrete problem, the discrete bilinear form is proven coercive and continuous, yielding an energy-error estimate of order h^{k+1} and an L²-error estimate of order h^{k+2}, with constants independent of compliancy parameters and mesh-interface position. Two-dimensional numerical experiments confirm predicted rates for k∈{1,2,3} and robustness over sixteen orders of magnitude of compliancy.
AI.conclusion: The unfitted HHO method provides a robust, provably convergent framework for elastic wave propagation across imperfect slipping interfaces, with high-order accuracy, parameter- and cut-independent error bounds, and effective coupling to Newmark and SDIRK time integrators.

title: An unstructured finite-volume Helmholtz method with perfectly matched layers for heterogeneous two-phase acoustics
comment: 41 pages, 19 figures, 7 tables; submitted to Computer Physics Communications
summary: This paper presents a cell-centred unstructured finite-volume method for time-harmonic two-phase acoustics. A volume-fraction representation supplies density and acoustic compressibility. Face fractions average available neighbouring planar interface cuts independently of velocity direction, retaining the established one-field face-density closure. Cartesian complex-coordinate stretching provides perfectly matched layers (PMLs). Real-imaginary splitting yields a real-valued block system, discretized with corrected non-orthogonal fluxes and consistent boundary contributions. Verification covers homogeneous waves, layered gas-liquid transmission with PML truncation, baffled-piston radiation with Kirchhoff far-field reconstruction, and resolved rigid-sphere radiation forces. Homogeneous-wave pressure converges at approximately second order on orthogonal meshes and on meshes with non-orthogonal interiors and orthogonal boundary cells. Reconstructed velocity converges at approximately second order on orthogonal meshes and with an observed order of about 1.7 on the latter mesh family. Under aligned refinement, the layered case's relative whole-domain complex-pressure $L_2$ error decreases to $2.657\times10^{-4}$. The resolved-sphere force differs from the Gorkov prediction by at most 1.5% over the tested Rayleigh size range. The results quantify the accuracy and current limitations of the heterogeneous Helmholtz-PML formulation.

AI.tldr: A cell-centred unstructured finite-volume method is developed for time-harmonic two-phase acoustics, using volume-fraction density/compressibility, PMLs, and real-imaginary splitting, verified across wave, transmission, radiation, and acoustic-force cases.
AI.motivation: There is a need for an accurate numerical method to solve heterogeneous time-harmonic (Helmholtz) acoustics in two-phase media, handling complex interfaces and unbounded domains.
AI.method: Cell-centred unstructured finite-volume scheme with volume-fraction representation of density and acoustic compressibility; face fractions average neighbouring planar interface cuts independent of velocity direction; Cartesian complex-coordinate stretching gives PMLs; real-imaginary splitting yields a real-valued block system discretized with corrected non-orthogonal fluxes and consistent boundary contributions.
AI.result: Homogeneous-wave pressure converges ~2nd order (orthogonal meshes; also non-orthogonal interiors with orthogonal boundary cells), velocity ~2nd order and ~1.7 observed order on latter. Layered case relative complex-pressure L2 error down to 2.657e-4 under aligned refinement. Resolved-sphere force within 1.5% of Gorkov prediction over tested Rayleigh range.
AI.conclusion: The results quantify the accuracy and current limitations of the heterogeneous Helmholtz-PML formulation for two-phase acoustics.

title: Theory of Equivalent Tokamaks for Characterizing Turbulent Transport in Quasi-symmetric Stellarators
summary: It is well known that quasi-symmetric (QS) stellarators are isomorphic to tokamaks in terms of their neoclassical-transport properties, and the corresponding transport coefficients can be calculated in the same manner as in tokamaks. However, less is known regarding the turbulent-transport properties of QS stellarators, e.g. the transport coefficients from the ion-temperature-gradient (ITG) mode. In this work, a systematic theory of the ``equivalent tokamaks'' for QS stellarators is presented based on the local gyrokinetic formulation and the near-axis expansion theory. It is shown that to zeroth order in the minor radius, the equivalent tokamaks can be chosen to have circular flux surfaces and can be characterized by three geometric quantities: the aspect ratio, the rotational transform, and the magnetic shear. To achieve first-order accuracy, however, not all QS stellarators have equivalent tokamaks, but good approximations can be found for some cases either as global or local equilibria. Local and global gyrokinetic simulations of ITG transport are performed for a selection of QS configurations, and quantitative agreement in the turbulent transport levels is found between the stellarators and their equivalent tokamaks.

AI.tldr: This work develops an "equivalent tokamak" theory for quasi-symmetric stellarators to predict turbulent (ITG) transport, showing quantitative agreement between QS stellarators and their equivalent tokamaks in gyrokinetic simulations.
AI.motivation: QS stellarators are known to be isomorphic to tokamaks for neoclassical transport, but their turbulent-transport properties (e.g., ITG-mode transport coefficients) are less understood. The paper aims to extend the equivalent-tokamak concept to turbulent transport.
AI.method: Systematic theory based on the local gyrokinetic formulation and near-axis expansion theory. Equivalent tokamaks are characterized by three geometric quantities: aspect ratio, rotational transform, and magnetic shear. Local and global gyrokinetic simulations of ITG transport are performed for selected QS configurations.
AI.result: To zeroth order in minor radius, equivalent tokamaks can have circular flux surfaces and are characterized by aspect ratio, rotational transform, and magnetic shear. To first order, not all QS stellarators have equivalent tokamaks, though good approximations exist for some cases (global or local equilibria). Simulations show quantitative agreement in turbulent transport levels between stellarators and their equivalent tokamaks.
AI.conclusion: The equivalent-tokamak framework extends to turbulent transport, allowing QS stellarator ITG transport to be approximated by a suitably defined tokamak, validated by gyrokinetic simulations.

title: Global Well-Posedness for Planar Compressible Magnetohydrodynamics with Degenerate Viscosity on Unbounded Domains
summary: The one-dimensional planar compressible magnetohydrodynamic system is studied on unbounded domains. The longitudinal viscosity obeys a power law of the specific volume, which permits it to degenerate as the density approaches vacuum, and the heat conductivity follows a power law of the temperature. For any fixed non-negative exponent in the heat conductivity term, the existence and uniqueness of global strong solutions are established for arbitrarily large initial data, provided that the positive exponent for viscosity is sufficiently small. The specific volume and temperature possess time-independent upper and lower bounds. Moreover, for each admissible viscosity exponent, the solution converges uniformly in space to the equilibrium state as time tends to infinity.

AI.tldr: Global strong solutions are proven for the 1D planar compressible MHD system on unbounded domains with degenerate viscosity and temperature-dependent heat conductivity, valid for arbitrarily large data when the viscosity exponent is small enough.
AI.motivation: The 1D planar compressible MHD system on unbounded domains involves degenerate viscosity (vanishing as density approaches vacuum) and power-law heat conductivity; establishing well-posedness and large-time behavior under such degeneracies and with large data is the goal.
AI.method: Analysis of the 1D planar compressible MHD system with longitudinal viscosity following a power law of specific volume and heat conductivity a power law of temperature; establishing a priori bounds and existence/uniqueness arguments for global strong solutions.
AI.result: For any fixed non-negative heat-conductivity exponent, when the viscosity exponent is sufficiently small, global strong solutions exist and are unique for arbitrarily large initial data; specific volume and temperature have time-independent upper and lower bounds; solutions converge uniformly in space to equilibrium as time tends to infinity.
AI.conclusion: The system admits global strong solutions with uniform-in-time bounds and large-time convergence to equilibrium across a range of admissible viscosity exponents.

title: Deterministic and stochastic particle methods for the Fokker-Planck equation in S--formulation with application to point set registration
summary: We present two particle methods for point set registration in bounded domains based on the Fokker-Planck equation. The first method relies on a moving least squares discretization of the S--formulation, in which moving grid points (particles) are advected by the drift with the target distribution, diffusion is resolved on a dynamically evolving particle cloud. This setting naturally leads to strong compression and expansion of the particle cloud. Obstacles are handled by enforcing reflective boundary conditions through a novel ghost point method. The second method is a Monte Carlo solver for the associated Langevin stochastic differential equation. It relies on a local approximation of the logarithmic gradient of the evolving particle density to extract macroscopic osmotic paths from individual stochastic trajectories. Owing to its inherent parallelism, this method exhibits excellent scalability and is well suited for high-dimensional registration problems. We illustrate the main features and performance of both approaches through extensive numerical experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two particle-based methods for point set registration in bounded domains using the Fokker-Planck equation: a moving least squares discretization of the S-formulation with ghost-point boundary handling, and a scalable Monte Carlo Langevin solver.
AI.motivation: Point set registration in bounded domains with obstacles is challenging, particularly when strong compression/expansion of particles occurs and when problems are high-dimensional. Existing approaches may struggle with boundary conditions and scalability.
AI.method: Two particle methods based on the Fokker-Planck equation. (1) A moving least squares discretization of the S-formulation: moving grid points (particles) advected by drift toward the target distribution, with diffusion resolved on a dynamically evolving cloud; obstacles handled by reflective boundary conditions via a novel ghost point method. (2) A Monte Carlo solver for the Langevin SDE, using a local approximation of the logarithmic gradient of the particle density to extract macroscopic osmotic paths from stochastic trajectories.
AI.result: Extensive numerical experiments illustrate the features and performance of both approaches. The Monte Carlo method shows excellent scalability due to inherent parallelism and suits high-dimensional registration.
AI.conclusion: Two complementary Fokker-Planck particle methods are provided for point set registration in bounded domains, combining accurate boundary handling with scalable high-dimensional performance.

title: Towards 3D fully randomized frequency-domain reconstruction of the speed of sound in breast ultrasound computed tomography
summary: Ultrasound computed tomography is emerging as a promising diagnostic imaging tool. 2D geometries suffer from notorious out-of-plane scattering artifacts. Image reconstruction can be achieved with frequency-domain full waveform inversion and it can be further accelerated by randomly phase-encoding the elementary sources. In this manuscript, we extend our previous results for the 2D geometry of a ring-array to the 3D cylindrical geometry of multiple rings. In particular, we consider the cases of an elementary source described by a single array element (quasi-omni-directional transmission), a line source and a focused transmission respectively. With differences in image quality, we prove that a fully randomized frequency-domain inversion in 3D is capable to reconstruct portions of a human breast surrounded by the cylindrical geometry and detect mm-size masses of varying contrast in dense breast, in reasonable computing times, thus opening the concrete possibility to the design of 3D imaging devices with high sensitivity levels. The methods are applicable to multiple tomographic geometries in 3D and, in principle, can be integrated into next generation medical ultrasound scanners.

AI.tldr: This paper extends 2D ring-array ultrasound computed tomography to 3D cylindrical multi-ring geometry, using frequency-domain full waveform inversion accelerated by random phase encoding, and shows it can reconstruct breast portions and detect mm-size masses in dense breast within reasonable computing times.
AI.motivation: 2D ultrasound computed tomography geometries suffer from out-of-plane scattering artifacts, motivating the need for 3D inversion to improve image quality and enable realistic imaging devices.
AI.method: The authors extend prior 2D ring-array results to a 3D cylindrical geometry of multiple rings. They use frequency-domain full waveform inversion with fully randomized phase encoding for acceleration, and consider three elementary source types: a single array element (quasi-omni-directional), a line source, and a focused transmission.
AI.result: Despite differences in image quality across source types, fully randomized frequency-domain 3D inversion reconstructs portions of a human breast surrounded by the cylindrical geometry and detects mm-size masses of varying contrast in dense breast, in reasonable computing times.
AI.conclusion: The approach opens the concrete possibility of designing 3D imaging devices with high sensitivity levels. The methods apply to multiple 3D tomographic geometries and can, in principle, be integrated into next-generation medical ultrasound scanners.

title: Derivative Embeddings in Vector-Valued Morrey Spaces
summary: We develop an intermediate-derivative theory for Banach-valued evolution classes with Morrey control in time. Let $E_0\hookrightarrow E$ be Banach spaces, $m\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, and $0\leλ<1$. If $u\in\mathcal M^{p,λ}(E_0)$ and $u^{(m)}\in\mathcal M^{p,λ}(E)$, then every intermediate derivative satisfies \[ u^{(j)}\in\mathcal M^{p,λ}\bigl((E_0,E)_{j/m,\infty}\bigr),\qquad 0<j<m, \] with no UMD, Fourier type, or operator-valued multiplier assumption. The proof is based on an exact rational-frequency splitting of $D^j$, the Peetre $K$-functional, and the Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator on Morrey spaces. On the line the estimate has the scale-sharp multiplicative form. On finite intervals we construct a graph-Morrey extension and obtain the same embedding. The weak fine index is optimal for arbitrary Banach couples. Combining the derivative theorem with the exact Morrey trace theorem yields an exact onto trace formula for every $u^{(j)}$, together with mixed Hölder/interpolation embeddings and a trace-powered $p$-to-$q$ Morrey gain. If $E_0\hookc E$, these embeddings become compact both in the same Morrey norm after an arbitrarily small loss of interpolation smoothness and in time-Hölder spaces above the derivative-trace threshold. For positive selfadjoint Hilbert scales we further improve the weak interpolation target to the fractional domain $D(B^{1-j/m})$ and show that this exponent is sharp.

AI.tldr: Intermediate-derivative theory for Banach-valued evolution classes with Morrey control in time, giving Morrey-valued embeddings for intermediate derivatives without UMD or Fourier-type assumptions.
AI.motivation: Existing intermediate-derivative and interpolation theories for Banach-valued evolution equations typically require UMD, Fourier type, or operator-valued multiplier assumptions, which exclude many Banach couples. The paper aims to remove such restrictions using Morrey control in time.
AI.method: Uses an exact rational-frequency splitting of D^j, the Peetre K-functional, and the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on Morrey spaces. Constructs a graph-Morrey extension on finite intervals. Combines with an exact Morrey trace theorem.
AI.result: If u in M^{p,λ}(E_0) and u^{(m)} in M^{p,λ}(E), then every intermediate derivative u^{(j)} lies in M^{p,λ}((E_0,E)_{j/m,∞}). The weak fine index is optimal for arbitrary Banach couples. Yields exact onto trace formulas, mixed Hölder/interpolation embeddings, and a trace-powered p-to-q Morrey gain. Compactness holds if E_0 compactly embeds in E. For selfadjoint Hilbert scales, target improves to D(B^{1-j/m}), shown sharp.
AI.conclusion: A hypothesis-light intermediate-derivative theory with sharp, scale-accurate Morrey embeddings, exact traces, compactness, and improved fractional-domain targets for Hilbert scales.

title: Toeplitz Infinite GMRES for Parameterized Linear Systems
summary: We develop Toeplitz infinite GMRES for solving large sparse analytic parameterized systems $A(s)x(s)=z$ at many parameter values. The method exploits a block upper triangular Toeplitz structure in the companion Krylov sequence to construct the Arnoldi process and recover solution approximations without storing full Arnoldi vectors. We derive incremental recurrences requiring $\mathcal{O}(np^2+p^3)$ arithmetic and $\mathcal{O}(np+p^2)$ storage for $p$ Arnoldi steps, excluding factorization setup and assuming linear-cost coefficient actions and triangular solves. A dynamic generator-refreshing strategy addresses cancellation in the basic recurrence. For matrix functions admitting a fixed separated representation, we further develop an implicitly rebased method based on a compact, contractive nilpotent matrix. Both variants preserve the Arnoldi process in exact arithmetic, with exact matrix-function actions required for the rebased method. A residual lower bound for square-summable Taylor coefficients explains a scaling obstruction outside the normalized unit disk. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Toeplitz infinite GMRES for solving large sparse analytic parameterized systems A(s)x(s)=z at many parameter values, exploiting block upper triangular Toeplitz structure in the companion Krylov sequence to make the Arnoldi process memory-efficient, with two variants and a theoretical scaling analysis.
AI.motivation: Solving large sparse analytic parameterized systems A(s)x(s)=z at many parameter values is computationally expensive. Standard GMRES requires storing full Arnoldi vectors and recomputing Krylov processes per parameter, which is inefficient when the companion Krylov sequence has exploitable structure.
AI.method: The method exploits block upper triangular Toeplitz structure in the companion Krylov sequence to build the Arnoldi process and recover solution approximations without storing full Arnoldi vectors. Incremental recurrences need O(np^2+p^3) arithmetic and O(np+p^2) storage for p Arnoldi steps. A dynamic generator-refreshing strategy handles cancellation in the basic recurrence. For matrix functions with a fixed separated representation, an implicitly rebased method is developed using a compact, contractive nilpotent matrix. Both variants preserve the Arnoldi process in exact arithmetic (the rebased method requires exact matrix-function actions).
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate computational efficiency. A residual lower bound for square-summable Taylor coefficients explains a scaling obstruction outside the normalized unit disk.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Toeplitz infinite GMRES methods offer efficient memory and arithmetic complexity for parameterized systems, with dynamic generator refreshing and an implicitly rebased variant for specific matrix functions, though scaling is limited outside the normalized unit disk.

title: BranchIP: Learning Adaptive Equivariant Computation for Interatomic Potentials
summary: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have revolutionized atomistic modeling, but accurate treatment of complex materials and molecular systems demands expensive models. This limits simulation length- and time-scales, with tensor products a key computational bottleneck. The recent emergence of foundation-scale MLIPs further exacerbates this challenge. We present Branch Interatomic Potential (BranchIP), a single-model framework for learned adaptive tensor product computation, trained with a novel distillation loss. In our experiments on two systems of physical interest, a heterogeneous catalysis system and a proton-conducting solid acid electrolyte, BranchIP accelerates MLIPs across model sizes by up to $2.4\times$ while reducing memory usage by up to $2.6\times$. This is achieved while maintaining physical fidelity. Furthermore, the learned adaptive computation provides model interpretability by revealing which interactions demand deeper computation and showing how computational depth relates to chemical complexity and dynamics.

AI.tldr: BranchIP is a single-model framework that learns adaptive tensor product computation for equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials, achieving up to 2.4x speedup and 2.6x memory reduction while preserving physical fidelity.
AI.motivation: Equivariant MLIPs enable accurate atomistic modeling but are computationally expensive, with tensor products as a key bottleneck. This limits simulation length- and time-scales, and the rise of foundation-scale MLIPs worsens the problem.
AI.method: The authors propose BranchIP, a single-model framework for learned adaptive tensor product computation, trained with a novel distillation loss.
AI.result: On a heterogeneous catalysis system and a proton-conducting solid acid electrolyte, BranchIP accelerates MLIPs across model sizes by up to 2.4x and reduces memory usage by up to 2.6x while maintaining physical fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The learned adaptive computation also provides interpretability, revealing which interactions require deeper computation and linking computational depth to chemical complexity and dynamics.

title: Quantitative schlieren imaging of a laser-ionized plasma channel in atomic vapor using symbolic regression
summary: The plasma channel of the AWAKE plasma wakefield acceleration experiment is created by laser ionization of rubidium vapor in a 10~m long vapor source. Verifying the properties of the channel --- the radius of its fully ionized core and the width of its boundary sheath --- that are vital for ensuring good-quality wakefields is important as is validating numerical models of ionizing pulse propagation. Near-resonant schlieren imaging can detect the plasma channel in the low-density vapor, but there is no direct inversion to obtain channel parameters from the images. We use symbolic regression to find compact analytical formulas that connect measurable properties of the schlieren signal to plasma profile parameters. Using databases of simulated signals generated with three different plasma edge-profile families, we obtain formulas with one and two fitting constants to predict the equivalent channel radius with an accuracy below twice the camera pixel size and formulas to predict the sheath width. Re-evaluating previous measurements with these formulas, we confirm a theoretically predicted power-law relationship between the channel radius and the energy of the ionizing laser pulse. The formulas can be adapted to new experimental conditions by refitting the constants on a modest set of new samples, providing a lightweight, interpretable alternative to evaluation with deep neural networks.

AI.tldr: Symbolic regression derives compact analytical formulas linking measurable schlieren signal properties to plasma channel parameters (radius and sheath width) in the AWAKE experiment, achieving sub-two-pixel accuracy and confirming a predicted power-law relationship.
AI.motivation: Verifying plasma channel properties (fully ionized core radius and boundary sheath width) is vital for good-quality wakefields, and validating ionization pulse propagation models matters. Near-resonant schlieren imaging can detect the channel in low-density vapor, but no direct inversion exists to extract channel parameters from images.
AI.method: Uses symbolic regression on databases of simulated schlieren signals generated with three different plasma edge-profile families to find compact analytical formulas with one and two fitting constants relating measurable signal properties to plasma profile parameters.
AI.result: Obtains formulas predicting equivalent channel radius with accuracy below twice the camera pixel size, plus formulas predicting sheath width. Re-evaluating prior measurements confirms a theoretically predicted power-law relationship between channel radius and ionizing laser pulse energy.
AI.conclusion: The formulas can be adapted to new experimental conditions by refitting constants on a modest set of new samples, providing a lightweight, interpretable alternative to deep neural network evaluation.

title: Critical anisotropic $p$-Laplace equations without finite energy: classification and a Schoen-type Harnack inequality
summary:
Let $N\ge 2$ and $1<p<N$. Let $H$ be a possibly non-reversible Minkowski norm on $\mathbb{R}^N$, with $H\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})$ and $D^2(H^2/2)$ uniformly positive definite away from the origin. We classify all nonnegative local weak solutions $u\in W^{1,p}_{m loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ of \[ -\operatorname{div} ig(H(
abla u)^{p-1}
abla H(
abla u) ig)=u^{p^*-1},\qquad p^*= rac{Np}{N-p}, \] without any finite-energy, integrability, or asymptotic assumption. Every nonzero solution is an anisotropic Sobolev bubble. This settles, for the full range $1<p<N$, the anisotropic analogue of Problem A of Antonini--Ciraolo--Gatti, whose Euclidean case was settled by Zhang, and removes the restriction on $p$ in the non-energy anisotropic classification of Chen--Wu--Yan--Yang. We also prove a scale-invariant Schoen-type Harnack inequality for local solutions.
  The proof follows the strategy of Zhang for the Euclidean $p$-Laplacian, combining rigidity of bounded blow-up profiles and a first-contact argument with the integral bootstrap of Ciraolo and Gatti. The anisotropic analysis requires two additional ingredients. First, we establish a Bochner identity for the conjugated stress tensor in distributional form on the noncritical set, using only $C^2$ regularity of $H$. Second, we prove a two-term expansion at isolated singularities of Finsler $p$-harmonic functions, including the gradient control needed by the Pohozaev invariant. For non-reversible anisotropies the argument is formulated with the reflected norm. A Morrey-type estimate proved directly for the relevant Leray--Lions operator replaces the potential-theoretic input used in the Euclidean argument.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies all nonnegative local weak solutions of a critical anisotropic p-Laplacian equation in R^N, showing every nonzero solution is an anisotropic Sobolev bubble, for the full range 1<p<N.
AI.motivation: This settles the anisotropic analogue of Problem A of Antonini–Ciraolo–Gatti for all p in (1,N), extending Zhang's Euclidean result and removing the p-restriction in the non-energy anisotropic classification of Chen–Wu–Yan–Yang, without any finite-energy or asymptotic assumptions.
AI.method: Follows Zhang's strategy for the Euclidean p-Laplacian, combining rigidity of bounded blow-up profiles and a first-contact argument with the integral bootstrap of Ciraolo–Gatti. Adds two anisotropic ingredients: a Bochner identity for the conjugated stress tensor in distributional form using only C^2 regularity of H, and a two-term expansion at isolated singularities of Finsler p-harmonic functions with gradient control for the Pohozaev invariant. Non-reversible anisotropies are handled via the reflected norm, and a Morrey-type estimate for the Leray–Lions operator replaces the potential-theoretic input.
AI.result: All nonzero nonnegative local weak solutions u in W^{1,p}_{loc}(R^N) are anisotropic Sobolev bubbles. A scale-invariant Schoen-type Harnack inequality for local solutions is also proved.
AI.conclusion: The classification is complete for the full range 1<p<N, and the anisotropic analogue of Problem A is resolved, alongside a new scale-invariant Harnack inequality.

title: Adaptive Multiresolution Diffusion Operators: A Variational Theory on Evolving Multiresolution Spaces
summary: We develop a variational framework for state-dependent diffusion on adaptive multiresolution representations in which the diffusion operator is generated by the adaptive state itself. The state consists of an admissible multiresolution tree, its active approximation space and basis, and the corresponding coefficient representation. It determines a symmetric nonnegative interaction form and an associated positive semidefinite intrinsic diffusion operator. In contrast to classical adaptive wavelet methods, where a prescribed operator is represented on an evolving approximation space, refinement and coarsening here modify simultaneously the representation, interaction graph, and operator. Because the adaptive hierarchy evolves through discrete topological changes, the coupled dynamics are formulated through a time-discrete variational principle rather than a differential evolution on a fixed space. We establish existence of the discrete updates, a discrete energy inequality, the coefficient-space null mode, and contractivity for frozen adaptive states. For regularized inverse problems, the construction yields Adaptive Multiresolution Diffusion Imaging (AMDI), combining data fidelity, intrinsic diffusion, coefficient sparsity, and tree complexity in a state-dependent energy. Numerical experiments verify the assembled operator identities, examine refinement-commutator decay, and confirm discrete energy dissipation. Adaptive Haar and higher-order multiwavelet calculations demonstrate localization of resolution on heterogeneous data. In denoising, AMDI retains high structural reconstruction quality with less than 10\% of the full active representation, with stable behavior across held-out noise realizations.

AI.tldr: A variational framework for state-dependent diffusion on adaptive multiresolution trees, where refinement/coarsening jointly modify representation, graph, and operator, leading to AMDI for imaging and denoising.
AI.motivation: Classical adaptive wavelet methods represent a prescribed operator on an evolving approximation space; here the operator itself is generated by the adaptive state, coupling representation, graph, and diffusion.
AI.method: Time-discrete variational principle on admissible multiresolution trees; state comprises tree, active basis, and coefficients, inducing a symmetric nonnegative interaction form and PSD intrinsic diffusion operator. Discrete updates, energy inequality, null mode, and contractivity for frozen states are established; AMDI combines data fidelity, intrinsic diffusion, coefficient sparsity, and tree complexity.
AI.result: Experiments verify operator identities, refinement-commutator decay, and discrete energy dissipation. Adaptive Haar/multiwavelet tests show resolution localization; denoising retains high structural quality with <10% of the full active representation, stable across held-out noise.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a principled adaptive, state-dependent diffusion scheme for inverse problems and imaging, enabling efficient multiresolution denoising with provable discrete properties.

title: A Nonlinear Two-Sheath Circuit Model for Low-Pressure Symmetric and Asymmetric Capacitively Coupled Radio-Frequency Plasmas
summary: We develop a nonlinear self-consistent two-sheath circuit model for low-pressure capacitively coupled plasmas that applies to geometrically symmetric as well as asymmetric discharges. The quasineutral plasma bulk is represented by an inductive-resistive element and coupled to stationary particle and electron-energy balances. Both boundary sheaths are treated dynamically using a lncosh sheath charge-voltage model with bounded differential elastance, based on a Riccati closure for the differential sheath width. The model recovers the quadratic depletion-sheath relation in the small-charge limit, while the characteristic sheath scales are determined from the RF-averaged sheath voltages using a collisionless Child-Langmuir/Bohm closure. The resulting four-variable RF subsystem contains the two sheath charges, the blocking-capacitor voltage, and the discharge current. In the symmetric monofrequent limit, the two sheath nonlinearities compensate strongly and the dc self-bias vanishes, whereas geometrical or electrical asymmetry breaks this compensation and enhances harmonic generation and plasma-series-resonance oscillations.

AI.tldr: A nonlinear self-consistent two-sheath circuit model for low-pressure capacitively coupled plasmas that captures symmetric and asymmetric discharges, recovering key sheath physics and asymmetry-driven effects.
AI.motivation: Existing models often fail to handle both geometrically symmetric and asymmetric capacitively coupled discharges within a unified, self-consistent framework that properly captures nonlinear sheath dynamics.
AI.method: The quasineutral bulk is modeled as an inductive-resistive element coupled to stationary particle and electron-energy balances. Both boundary sheaths use a lncosh charge-voltage model with bounded differential elastance via a Riccati closure for the differential sheath width. Sheath scales come from RF-averaged sheath voltages using a collisionless Child-Langmuir/Bohm closure. The RF subsystem has four variables: two sheath charges, blocking-capacitor voltage, and discharge current.
AI.result: The model recovers the quadratic depletion-sheath relation in the small-charge limit. In the symmetric monofrequent case, the two sheath nonlinearities compensate strongly, giving zero dc self-bias. Geometric or electrical asymmetry breaks this compensation, enhancing harmonic generation and plasma-series-resonance oscillations.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a self-consistent, physically grounded description of sheath dynamics applicable to both symmetric and asymmetric CCP discharges, linking asymmetry to enhanced harmonics and series-resonance behavior.

title: Phase transition, sharp asymptotics and symmetry for critical quasilinear Hartree equations beyond $σ=2p$
summary: We establish the sharp asymptotic and symmetry theory for the critical quasilinear Hartree equation \[ -Δ_pu=\big(|x|^{-σ}*u^{p^*_σ}\big)u^{p^*_σ-1} \quad\text{in }\mathbb R^N, \qquad p^*_σ=\frac{p(2N-σ)}{2(N-p)}, \] in the complementary range $2p<σ<N$, beyond the quasilinear theory previously available for $σ\le2p$ [Math. Ann., 391(2):2653--2708, 2025]. This range is structurally different: $p^*_σ<p$, so the effective potential obtained by factoring out $u^{p-1}$ becomes singular as $u\to0$. Nevertheless, whenever $p^*_σ>1$, every nonnegative finite-energy weak solution is automatically locally bounded. Our proof provides a quasilinear regularity mechanism adapted to this complementary range, where the potential-theoretic route available for $σ\le2p$ breaks down. For positive finite-energy solutions with $p^*_σ>1$ we moreover uncover a sharp transition governed by the sign of $σ(p-2)+2p$. If this quantity is positive, the classical $p$-harmonic profile persists. At the threshold, \[ u(x)\simeq |x|^{-γ_h}(\log|x|)^{1/(p-p^*_σ)}, \qquad γ_h=\frac{N-p}{p-1}, \] with the matching two-sided gradient rate. Below the threshold, \[ u(x)=A_*|x|^{-γ_*}+o(|x|^{-γ_*}), \qquad γ_*=\frac{2(N-p)(σ-p)}{p(σ-2p)}<γ_h, \] and the rescaled gradients converge uniformly to the corresponding radial profile. In all three regimes the solutions are radially symmetric about some point and strictly decreasing in the radial variable.

AI.tldr: Sharp asymptotics and symmetry for the critical quasilinear Hartree equation are established in the complementary range 2p < σ < N, revealing a trichotomy in the asymptotic profile governed by the sign of σ(p−2)+2p.
AI.motivation: Prior quasilinear theory only covered σ ≤ 2p. The complementary range 2p < σ < N is structurally different: p*_σ < p, so the effective potential obtained by factoring out u^{p−1} becomes singular as u→0, and the potential-theoretic route breaks down, requiring new methods.
AI.method: A quasilinear regularity mechanism adapted to the complementary range shows that whenever p*_σ > 1, every nonnegative finite-energy weak solution is locally bounded. For positive finite-energy solutions with p*_σ > 1, the sharp asymptotic profiles are derived by analyzing the sign of σ(p−2)+2p, including the threshold logarithmic correction and the sub-threshold power rate via rescaled gradients.
AI.result: A sharp trichotomy: (i) if σ(p−2)+2p > 0, the classical p-harmonic profile persists; (ii) at the threshold, u ≈ |x|^{−γ_h}(log|x|)^{1/(p−p*_σ)} with matching two-sided gradient rate; (iii) below the threshold, u = A_*|x|^{−γ_*}+o(|x|^{−γ_*}) with γ_* < γ_h, and rescaled gradients converge uniformly to the radial profile.
AI.conclusion: In all three regimes, solutions are radially symmetric about some point and strictly decreasing in the radial variable, completing the sharp asymptotic and symmetry theory for the critical quasilinear Hartree equation beyond previously available ranges.

title: Approximation and computation of the geodesic Sinkhorn distance
summary: In [H. Lavenant, J. Luckhardt, G. Mordant, B. Schmitzer, L. Tamanini, The Riemannian geometry of Sinkhorn divergences. Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré Anal. Non Linéaire 43 (2026)] we introduced a Riemannian metric $\mathsf{d}_S$ on the space of probability distributions obtained from entropic optimal transport, specifically from the Sinkhorn divergence $S_\varepsilon$. In the present work we discuss how to approximate and compute $\mathsf{d}_S$. Spatially, we prove Gromov--Hausdorff convergence of the metric and convergence of geodesics for increasingly fine Eulerian discretization of the base space. Temporally, we show $Γ$-convergence of the chain discretization $N \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} S_\varepsilon(μ_k, μ_{k+1})$ to the energy functional defining $\mathsf{d}_S$. We deduce and implement numerical schemes to compute approximations of $\mathsf{d}_S$.

AI.tldr: This work develops approximation and computation methods for the Sinkhorn divergence-based Riemannian metric d_S, proving Gromov–Hausdorff convergence under spatial discretization and Γ-convergence under temporal (chain) discretization, and implementing numerical schemes.
AI.motivation: A prior work introduced a Riemannian metric d_S on the space of probability distributions derived from entropic optimal transport via the Sinkhorn divergence S_ε. However, how to practically approximate and compute this metric remained open.
AI.method: Spatially, proves Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of the metric and of geodesics for increasingly fine Eulerian discretizations of the base space. Temporally, shows Γ-convergence of the chain discretization N Σ S_ε(μ_k, μ_{k+1}) to the energy functional defining d_S. Numerical schemes are then deduced and implemented.
AI.result: Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of the metric and geodesics is established spatially; Γ-convergence of the chain discretization to the energy functional is established temporally, yielding implementable numerical schemes for approximating d_S.
AI.conclusion: The Sinkhorn divergence metric d_S can be reliably approximated and computed via the developed discretization results and numerical schemes.

title: Analysis of grid instabilities in particle-in-cell codes based on a meshfree approach
summary: A new method of analyzing grid, or aliasing, instabilities is described, in particle-in-cell (PIC) codes for plasma kinetic theory. It starts with a meshfree approach with $N_{p}$ macroparticles, with $N_{p}<\infty$. Linearization of these equations is done about a uniform density non-drifting equilibrium prescribed by macroparticles on a uniform \emph{lattice}. Macroparticle positions perturbations are induced about this lattice. The resulting linear equations are analyzed for stability and dispersion relations. The linearized equations are then discretized on a grid of $N_{g}$ points with $N_{g} \le N_{p}$, in both momentum conserving (MCP) and energy conserving (ECP) formulations. For a cold stationary plasma, this leads a \emph{dynamical matrix}. For ECP, the matrix is symmetric and positive definite (SPD) and immediately shows stability. For MCP, the dynamical matrix is neither symmetric nor positive definite, preventing immediate conclusions on stability. For both MCP and ECP and for a cold stationary plasma, the resulting matrix elements vary relative to the meshfree value, a result of aliasing. This deviation is periodic in the displacement of the particle lattice relative to the grid. In the MCP discretization, eigenvalues occur in complex conjugate pairs for general placement of the particle lattice relative to the grid. These conjugate pairs indicate nonnegative growth rates. The nature of the aliasing is studied and shown to be related to the trapezoidal rule error over the grid. The scaling of the linear growth rates with respect to $N_{g}$ and especially with respect to $N_{ppc}$ is studied. These analytical results are compared with PIC simulations and found to be in excellent agreement. The connection with a cold drifting \emph{beam} is discussed briefly, specifically, grid-induced instabilities for both the MCP and ECP.

AI.tldr: A new meshfree-to-grid linear stability analysis of PIC grid (aliasing) instabilities, showing MCP schemes yield complex-conjugate eigenvalues with nonnegative growth rates while ECP is stable (SPD), with growth rates scaling versus Ng and Nppc validated against simulations.
AI.motivation: Grid (aliasing) instabilities in particle-in-cell codes for plasma kinetic theory are poorly understood analytically; a systematic method is needed to isolate how discretizing to a grid introduces aliasing and destabilizes otherwise stable equilibria, particularly distinguishing momentum-conserving (MCP) from energy-conserving (ECP) formulations.
AI.method: Starts with a meshfree PIC formulation of Np macroparticles at finite Np, linearized about a uniform non-drifting equilibrium prescribed on a uniform lattice with position perturbations. The resulting linear equations are analyzed for dispersion and stability, then discretized on a grid of Ng points (Ng ≤ Np) in both MCP and ECP formulations. For a cold stationary plasma this yields a dynamical matrix: SPD for ECP, non-symmetric/non-positive-definite for MCP. Aliasing deviations are studied and linked to the trapezoidal-rule error; growth-rate scaling with Ng and Nppc is derived and compared to PIC simulations; connection to a cold drifting beam is discussed.
AI.result: For ECP the dynamical matrix is SPD, immediately implying stability. For MCP it is neither symmetric nor positive definite, so stability cannot be concluded immediately. For both schemes the matrix elements deviate from the meshfree values due to aliasing, with deviations periodic in the particle-lattice displacement relative to the grid. In MCP, eigenvalues appear in complex-conjugate pairs for general lattice placement, indicating nonnegative growth rates. The aliasing is shown to relate to the trapezoidal-rule error over the grid, and linear growth rates scale with Ng and especially Nppc. Analytical results agree excellently with PIC simulations.
AI.conclusion: The meshfree linearization with lattice perturbations provides a clean framework for analyzing grid/aliasing instabilities. MCP formulations can exhibit grid-induced instabilities (conjugate eigenvalue pairs, nonnegative growth), whereas ECP remains stable (SPD) for a cold stationary plasma. The work further discusses grid-induced instabilities for a cold drifting beam in both MCP and ECP.

title: A Liouville theorem for the real twisted Monge-Ampère equation
summary: We establish a Pogorelov type interior $C^2$ estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampere equation without assuming uniform ellipticity. This equation is fully nonlinear and elliptic, but is neither concave nor a function of the eigenvalues of the Hessian, so the standard techniques for interior second-derivative estimates do not directly apply. Building on the partial Legendre transform formulation of Streets and Warren, we derive a differential identity for the associated positive-definite matrix $W(D^2u)$ and use some linear algebra to control the third-order terms arising in the maximum principle argument. As an application, we prove a Liouville theorem for entire split convex solutions with quadratic growth, extending the rigidity theorem of Streets and Warren by replacing their uniform ellipticity hypothesis with suitable quadratic growth assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a Pogorelov-type interior C² estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampère equation without uniform ellipticity, using a partial Legendre transform and a differential identity for the matrix W(D²u), and derives a Liouville theorem for entire split convex solutions with quadratic growth.
AI.motivation: The real twisted Monge-Ampère equation is fully nonlinear and elliptic but is neither concave nor a function of Hessian eigenvalues, so standard techniques for interior second-derivative estimates do not apply. Moreover, existing rigidity results (Streets–Warren) rely on a uniform ellipticity hypothesis that the authors aim to relax.
AI.method: Building on the partial Legendre transform formulation of Streets and Warren, the authors derive a differential identity for the associated positive-definite matrix W(D²u), then use linear algebra to control the third-order terms arising in the maximum principle argument.
AI.result: They establish a Pogorelov-type interior C² estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampère equation without assuming uniform ellipticity.
AI.conclusion: As an application, they prove a Liouville theorem for entire split convex solutions with quadratic growth, extending the rigidity theorem of Streets and Warren by replacing their uniform ellipticity hypothesis with suitable quadratic growth assumptions.

title: Entropy dissipative high order schemes for a hyperbolic model of two-layer thin film flow
summary: In this article, we develop high-order, entropy-dissipative schemes for a hyperbolic system of conservation laws describing the first-order dynamics of two-layer thin-film flows of immiscible fluids with perfectly soluble solute particles. The key aspect is to construct entropy-conservative fluxes in the sense of Tadmor. Here, we consider and compare two different construction processes: an exact formulation and a commonly used simplified approximation in the flux evaluation. While the approximate approach is simpler at the level of construction and is frequently employed in practice (also in other contexts), it is less structured, leading to increased computational cost in the implementation compared to the exact formulation, which has been much more complicated to derive. We employ these fluxes within both an entropy-dissipative finite-difference framework and an entropy-dissipative discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method. Through numerical experiments using two distinct spatial discretizations, we investigate the performance and robustness of the proposed methods and demonstrate that the choice of numerical flux has a noticeable impact on the efficiency of the resulting solvers.

AI.tldr: This paper develops high-order, entropy-dissipative schemes for a two-layer thin-film flow system with soluble solutes, comparing exact vs. approximate entropy-conservative fluxes within finite-difference and DG spectral element frameworks.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to construct entropy-conservative fluxes (Tadmor sense) for a hyperbolic conservation law modeling two-layer immiscible thin-film flows with perfectly soluble solute particles, and to clarify how the choice between exact and simplified flux formulations affects solver efficiency.
AI.method: Two entropy-conservative flux construction processes are considered and compared: an exact formulation and a commonly used simplified approximation in flux evaluation. These fluxes are embedded in two entropy-dissipative frameworks: a finite-difference scheme and a discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method.
AI.result: The approximate approach is simpler to construct and widely used, but is less structured, leading to higher computational cost in implementation compared to the exact formulation, despite the latter being harder to derive. Numerical experiments with two distinct spatial discretizations show the choice of numerical flux noticeably impacts solver efficiency and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The choice of numerical flux has a noticeable impact on solver efficiency; the exact entropy-conservative formulation, though more complex to derive, offers better-structured and more efficient implementation than the simplified approximation.

title: Birth-Potential Multigroup Fluid Model for Ballistic Electrons: Breakdown and Cathode Sheath Regimes
summary: Fluid models of discharges fail where electron runaway dominates. On the left branch of the Paschen curve and in high-voltage cathode sheaths, the electron population splits into a thermal bulk and a ballistic beam that no single electron fluid can represent. We present a multigroup fluid model that divides ballistic electrons into groups indexed by their birth potential: the electrostatic potential at which they were liberated, offset by the forward kinetic energy they carried. Because the birth potential is a constant of ballistic motion, the electric field never moves electrons between groups and only collisions do. Each group requires a single continuity equation because its velocity follows algebraically from the local potential, and the number of groups is set by the energy resolution alone independently of the mesh. A runaway criterion based on the local field assigns each newly liberated electron to the bulk or a ballistic group, so the model applies even where no sheath exists. Benchmarked against a kinetic solver in argon, it reproduces the left branch of the Paschen curve---which local-field and local-energy models miss or misplace---and tracks the current--voltage characteristic of a cathode sheath to within a few percent at reduced fields exceeding $10^4$ Td, where the local-energy model overpredicts the current up to thirtyfold. Since as few as 10 to 30 groups suffice, depending on the field, the approach brings near-kinetic accuracy to multi-species computational fluid dynamics solvers at the cost of that many additional species, without added velocity-space dimensions or particle noise.

AI.tldr: A multigroup fluid model represents ballistic (runaway) electrons by groups indexed by birth potential, reproducing the left Paschen branch and cathode-sheath I-V curves where conventional fluid models fail.
AI.motivation: Standard fluid discharge models fail when electron runaway dominates, as on the left Paschen branch and in high-voltage cathode sheaths. There the electron population splits into a thermal bulk and a ballistic beam that no single electron fluid can represent. Local-field and local-energy models either miss or misplace the left branch and drastically overpredict sheath current.
AI.method: Divide ballistic electrons into groups indexed by birth potential (the electrostatic potential at liberation offset by forward kinetic energy). Because birth potential is a constant of ballistic motion, the field never transfers electrons between groups; only collisions do. Each group needs only one continuity equation since its velocity follows algebraically from the local potential, and group count is set by energy resolution, independent of the mesh. A local-field runaway criterion assigns each newly liberated electron to the bulk or a ballistic group, so the model works even without a sheath.
AI.result: Benchmarked against a kinetic solver in argon, the model reproduces the left branch of the Paschen curve---which local-field and local-energy models miss or misplace---and tracks the cathode-sheath current-voltage characteristic to within a few percent at reduced fields above 10^4 Td, where the local-energy model overpredicts current up to thirtyfold. Only 10 to 30 groups suffice depending on the field.
AI.conclusion: The multigroup approach brings near-kinetic accuracy to multi-species CFD solvers at the cost of 10-30 extra species, with no added velocity-space dimensions or particle noise.

title: Ill-posedness in the critical Sobolev space for the hyperelastic rod equation
summary:
This article is the third in a series investigating ill-posedness in critical Sobolev spaces for Camassa-Holm-type equations. Following results for the $b$-Novikov and Fokas-Olver-Rosenau-Qiao equations, we study the hyperelastic rod equation at the critical Sobolev regularity $H^{3/2}(\mathbb R)$. We prove ill-posedness at this endpoint, complementing the local well-posedness theory in $H^s(\mathbb R)$ for $s>3/2$ and the recently established norm-inflation result for $1<s<3/2$.
  The nature of the critical ill-posedness depends on the parameter $γ$. For $0<γ\leq3$, we construct arbitrarily small smooth initial data whose corresponding solutions develop finite-time blow-up, with the maximal lifespan tending to zero with the size of the initial data. For $γ<0$ or $γ>3$, we construct solutions with arbitrarily small $H^{3/2}$ initial data whose $H^{3/2}$ norm becomes arbitrarily large in arbitrarily short time.

AI.tldr: This paper proves ill-posedness of the hyperelastic rod equation at the critical Sobolev regularity H^{3/2}(R), completing a series on ill-posedness in critical spaces for Camassa-Holm-type equations. The type of ill-posedness depends on the parameter gamma.
AI.motivation: This is the third in a series investigating ill-posedness in critical Sobolev spaces for Camassa-Holm-type equations. Previous works handled the b-Novikov and Fokas-Olver-Rosenau-Qiao equations; the hyperelastic rod equation at the critical regularity H^{3/2} remained open. The goal is to complement the known local well-posedness for s>3/2 and the norm-inflation result for 1<s<3/2.
AI.method: The analysis is carried out at the critical Sobolev regularity H^{3/2}(R) for the hyperelastic rod equation. Different constructions of initial data are used depending on the parameter gamma: smooth small data leading to finite-time blow-up for 0<gamma<=3, and small H^{3/2} data whose norm grows arbitrarily fast for gamma<0 or gamma>3.
AI.result: Ill-posedness is proven at the endpoint H^{3/2}. For 0<gamma<=3, arbitrarily small smooth initial data yield solutions with finite-time blow-up, with maximal lifespan tending to zero as the data size vanishes. For gamma<0 or gamma>3, arbitrarily small H^{3/2} initial data produce solutions whose H^{3/2} norm becomes arbitrarily large in arbitrarily short time.
AI.conclusion: The hyperelastic rod equation is ill-posed at the critical Sobolev regularity H^{3/2}(R), with the nature of the ill-posedness (blow-up vs. immediate norm inflation) determined by the parameter gamma. This completes the critical-space ill-posedness picture alongside local well-posedness for s>3/2 and norm inflation for 1<s<3/2.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Free-Boundary Partial Differential Equations
summary: We study free-boundary problems within a physics-informed framework using Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) approximations. The proposed approach incorporates obstacle constraints, partial differential equation (PDE) inequalities, complementarity conditions, and boundary conditions through residual-based loss functions. We consider a linear elliptic obstacle problem, a nonlinear $p$-Laplacian obstacle problem, and a time-dependent one-phase Stefan problem. The proposed KAN solver is compared with physics-informed neural network (PINN) and residual-network baselines. Numerical experiments show that KANs achieve low relative $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ errors while accurately resolving contact regions and moving interfaces. The results indicate that KAN representations provide an effective alternative for solving free-boundary PDEs.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to solve free-boundary PDE problems, showing KANs outperform PINN and residual-network baselines in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Free-boundary problems (obstacle, p-Laplacian, Stefan problems) are challenging for traditional solvers due to unknown contact regions and moving interfaces, motivating a physics-informed approach with a flexible approximator.
AI.method: A physics-informed KAN solver encodes obstacle constraints, PDE inequalities, complementarity conditions, and boundary conditions via residual-based loss functions. It is applied to a linear elliptic obstacle problem, a nonlinear p-Laplacian obstacle problem, and a time-dependent one-phase Stefan problem, compared against PINN and residual-network baselines.
AI.result: KANs achieve low relative L2 and L∞ errors, accurately resolving contact regions and moving interfaces, outperforming PINN and residual-network baselines.
AI.conclusion: KAN representations offer an effective alternative for solving free-boundary PDEs.

title: Teaching a plasma physics and engineering class at a liberal arts college using Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs)
summary: Undergraduate research experiences provide students with an opportunity to apply knowledge learned in the classroom to authentic scientific problems. In this work, we describe the development of a special-topics course in Plasma Physics and Engineering (PPE) at a small liberal arts college using a Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs). During the first half of the semester, students learned fundamental plasma physics and dusty plasma concepts through traditional lectures and homework. During the second half, they applied this knowledge to investigate an unanswered research question: why does the levitation time of growing nanoparticles decrease in the presence of a magnetic field? Students learned and used Langmuir probe and optical emission spectroscopy diagnostics to characterize an argon plasma over a range of magnetic-field strengths. Their measurements showed a general decrease in electron density with increasing magnetic field strength, while optical emission measurements confirmed a reduction in carbonaceous nanoparticle growth-cycle time from acetylene. Using the measured plasma parameters, students estimated the nanoparticle charge and developed the hypothesis that a reduction in electron density leads to a smaller negative dust charge and consequently a weaker electric force available to levitate the particles as a function of increasing magnetic field strength between 50 and 330 Gauss. Students subsequently disseminated their results through research poster presentations at conferences. Course evaluations and E-CLASS responses also indicated positive student experiences with the laboratory and research components of the course. This work demonstrates one approach for integrating plasma physics education and authentic research in an undergraduate curriculum at a small liberal arts institution.

AI.tldr: A special-topics Plasma Physics and Engineering course at a small liberal arts college used a CURE model to give undergraduates authentic research experience investigating why nanoparticle levitation time decreases under a magnetic field.
AI.motivation: Undergraduate research experiences let students apply classroom knowledge to real scientific problems, and this work aims to integrate plasma physics education with authentic research in a small liberal arts curriculum.
AI.method: First half of the semester: traditional lectures and homework on fundamental plasma and dusty plasma concepts. Second half: students used Langmuir probe and optical emission spectroscopy to characterize an argon plasma across magnetic-field strengths, measuring electron density and carbonaceous nanoparticle growth-cycle time.
AI.result: Electron density generally decreased with increasing magnetic field strength, and optical emission confirmed reduced nanoparticle growth-cycle time. Students hypothesized that lower electron density yields smaller negative dust charge, weakening the electric levitation force for fields between 50 and 330 Gauss. Students presented posters at conferences, and course evaluations plus E-CLASS responses were positive.
AI.conclusion: The course demonstrates a feasible approach for integrating plasma physics education and authentic research into an undergraduate curriculum at a small liberal arts institution.

title: Optimal multipolar Lp-Hardy inequalities: ground states, criticality, and variational thresholds
summary: We study the relation between ground states, criticality, and variational compactness for a family of genuinely multipolar Lp-Hardy weights, 1 < p < n. A ground-state representation valid across the poles gives a complete classification of the full potential into critical and subcritical parameter regions and distinguishes finite-energy attainment from non-attained criticality. Removing a geometric interaction term leads to a second variational problem, whose optimal coefficient is controlled by concentration at the poles and at infinity. We prove that a strict gap below the resulting threshold yields strong compactness of normalized minimizing sequences, a positive extremizer, and criticality of the optimally rescaled operator. For 1 < p < 2, this gap holds throughout the full-potential critical set and the optimal truncated coefficient is strictly below 1; for p >2, the coefficient is strictly above 1 in the full-potential attainment region. At fixed parameters strictly inside the quadratic attained region, the optimal value converges to 1 as p tending to 2, with attainment and criticality on both sides. The proofs combine null sequence rigidity and strict-pole capacity with local weighted compactness across the zero set of the underlying vector field.

AI.tldr: The paper links ground states, criticality, and variational compactness for genuinely multipolar Lp-Hardy weights (1<p<n), classifying the potential into critical/subcritical regions and proving compactness, existence of extremizers, and p→2 behavior.
AI.motivation: To understand how ground-state representations relate to criticality and variational compactness for multipolar Lp-Hardy weights, and to distinguish finite-energy attainment from non-attained criticality.
AI.method: A ground-state representation valid across the poles classifies the full potential into critical and subcritical regions. A second variational problem is introduced by removing a geometric interaction term; its optimal coefficient is controlled by concentration at poles and infinity. Proofs combine null sequence rigidity, strict-pole capacity, and local weighted compactness across the zero set of the underlying vector field.
AI.result: A strict gap below the threshold yields strong compactness of normalized minimizing sequences, a positive extremizer, and criticality of the optimally rescaled operator. For 1<p<2, the gap holds throughout the full-potential critical set and the optimal truncated coefficient is strictly below 1; for p>2, the coefficient is strictly above 1 in the full-potential attainment region. At fixed parameters strictly inside the quadratic attained region, the optimal value converges to 1 as p→2, with attainment and criticality on both sides.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a complete criticality/attainment classification for multipolar Lp-Hardy weights and establish sharp compactness criteria with distinct p<2 and p>2 regimes, recovering the quadratic case as p→2.

title: Multifidelity Formulations for Triangular Transport
summary: We develop multifidelity methods for constructing triangular transport maps from samples, when high-fidelity data are scarce but lower-fidelity data are more abundant. Using this set of multifidelity data, we approximate a triangular transport map that bijectively maps between a tractable reference density and the high-fidelity target distribution. We introduce two strategies to leverage low-fidelity data: a hierarchical approach that composes maps between adjacent fidelity levels, and a non-hierarchical method that incorporates low-fidelity information through monotonicity-preserving corrections to the map parameterization. Numerical experiments compare these strategies with single-fidelity transport and demonstrate how the proposed multifidelity approaches can improve map estimation from limited high-fidelity data. To illustrate the broader utility of the learned maps, we also deploy them in a downstream amortized simulation-based inference task. This example shows that multifidelity improvements in map estimation can translate to improved conditional sampling and uncertainty quantification when high-fidelity data are scarce.

AI.tldr: Multifidelity methods for learning triangular transport maps using abundant low-fidelity and scarce high-fidelity samples, with two strategies (hierarchical and non-hierarchical) improving map estimation and downstream inference.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity data are scarce, but lower-fidelity data are more abundant; the goal is to leverage this cost asymmetry to better estimate a transport map that maps a reference density to the high-fidelity target distribution.
AI.method: Two strategies: (1) a hierarchical approach that composes maps between adjacent fidelity levels, and (2) a non-hierarchical method that incorporates low-fidelity information via monotonicity-preserving corrections to the map parameterization. Both approximate a triangular transport map bijectively mapping a tractable reference density to the high-fidelity target.
AI.result: Numerical experiments compare both strategies against single-fidelity transport and show that multifidelity approaches improve map estimation from limited high-fidelity data. Applied to downstream amortized simulation-based inference, the gains translate to improved conditional sampling and uncertainty quantification when high-fidelity data are scarce.
AI.conclusion: Multifidelity transport map learning effectively exploits cheap low-fidelity data to enhance estimation of high-fidelity distributions and benefits downstream inference and uncertainty quantification.

title: Femtosecond laser-induced cavitation seeds liquid-jet breakup beyond the Rayleigh-Plateau stability limit
summary: The Rayleigh-Plateau instability predicts that infinitesimal perturbations of a liquid jet grow only for kR < 1, with kR = 1 marking the classical stability boundary. Here, we show that femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation generates a localized, impulsive recoil perturbation on a flowing liquid jet, enabling a two-dimensional map of jet breakup across the (kR, epsilon/R) plane. The perturbation's spacing (wavelength) and strength (amplitude) are set independently by the laser repetition rate and pulse energy, respectively. At low amplitudes, tuning the repetition rate recovers the classical Rayleigh-Plateau dispersion relation and its kR = 1 cutoff, while increasing the wavelength enables controlled generation of monodisperse droplet trains, bidisperse droplet populations, and ultimately isolated single droplets. Along the amplitude axis, low pulse energies produce a seed that amplifies only the imposed wavenumber, whereas above a critical energy Ec, the seed broadens to excite many wavenumbers simultaneously. At still higher amplitudes, we demonstrate deterministic breakup for kR > 1, extending to kR = 1.9, with laser-synchronized droplet production rates up to 0.2 MHz. These results establish localized femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation as a route to controlled Rayleigh-Plateau breakup both within and beyond the classical linear-stability boundary.

AI.tldr: Femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation on a flowing jet gives a 2D map of Rayleigh-Plateau breakup, enabling deterministic breakup even beyond the classical kR = 1 boundary (up to kR = 1.9) with droplet rates to 0.2 MHz.
AI.motivation: Classical Rayleigh-Plateau theory limits instability growth to kR < 1, which restricts controllable jet breakup. The authors seek a way to manipulate breakup wavelength and amplitude independently and to break past this stability boundary.
AI.method: A femtosecond laser induces localized cavitation, producing an impulsive recoil perturbation on a flowing liquid jet. Wavelength is set by laser repetition rate and perturbation strength by pulse energy, giving an independent 2D (kR, epsilon/R) map.
AI.result: At low amplitude the classical dispersion relation and kR = 1 cutoff are recovered; varying wavelength yields monodisperse trains, bidisperse populations, and single droplets. Above E_c the seed excites many wavenumbers. Deterministic breakup is shown for kR > 1 up to 1.9, with rates up to 0.2 MHz.
AI.conclusion: Localized femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation is a versatile route to controlled Rayleigh-Plateau breakup both within and beyond the classical linear-stability boundary.

title: Global weak varifold solutions to Navier-Stokes/Mean Curvature Flow system
summary: The Navier-Stokes/Mean Curvature Flow system describes a two-phase flow of incompressible, viscous and immiscible fluids separated by a sharp interface, whose evolution is governed by a convective mean curvature flow equation, coupled to a two-phase Navier-Stokes equation accounting for surface tension. Among others, this model describes the dynamics of dry foams and it also arises as a sharp interface limit of Navier-Stokes/Allen-Cahn systems with non-vanishing mobility. Despite this wide range of applications, global-in-time existence of any kind of weak solutions remains a challenging open problem. In this work, we introduce a novel notion of varifold weak solution in two and three ambient dimensions, based on a sharp energy dissipation principle à la De Giorgi, and we show for the first time the unconditional global-in-time existence of such a weak solution. We also show, by means of a relative entropy approach, that any classical solution to the Navier-Stokes/Mean Curvature Flow system is unique in the class of our new weak varifold solutions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new notion of varifold weak solution for the Navier-Stokes/Mean Curvature Flow system in 2D and 3D and proves unconditional global-in-time existence, plus uniqueness of classical solutions within this class via a relative entropy approach.
AI.motivation: The Navier-Stokes/Mean Curvature Flow system models two-phase flows of incompressible, viscous, immiscible fluids with a sharp interface (e.g., dry foams, sharp interface limit of Navier-Stokes/Allen-Cahn systems). Despite wide applications, global-in-time existence of weak solutions was an open problem.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel notion of varifold weak solution in two and three ambient dimensions, based on a sharp energy dissipation principle in the style of De Giorgi. They use a relative entropy approach to address uniqueness.
AI.result: The paper shows for the first time the unconditional global-in-time existence of such weak varifold solutions. It also proves that any classical solution to the system is unique within the class of these new weak varifold solutions.
AI.conclusion: A new weak solution framework (varifold-based) resolves the open problem of global-in-time existence for the Navier-Stokes/Mean Curvature Flow system and provides a uniqueness result for classical solutions in this class.

title: On the Pricing of American Options under Stochastic Local Volatility and Stochastic Correlation via the RBSDE Framework
summary: In this work, we study the pricing of American options under stochastic local volatility (SLV) models extended by including stochastic correlation driven by an additional stochastic process. We generalize the class of SLV models by incorporating a flexible stochastic correlation structure. To price options within these extended models, we derive the corresponding reflected forward-backward stochastic differential equations (RBSDEs) and employ data-driven numerical methods to solve them for both pricing and hedging purposes. The RBSDE framework enables the modelling of the future evolution of the option price. Furthermore, we conduct a convergence analysis of the proposed numerical method and present numerical experiments that illustrate the performance of the extended models, as well as the accuracy and efficiency of the RBSDE-based approach.

AI.tldr: This paper prices American options under stochastic local volatility (SLV) models extended with flexible stochastic correlation, using reflected forward-backward SDEs (RBSDEs) solved by data-driven numerical methods for pricing and hedging.
AI.motivation: Standard SLV models lack a flexible stochastic correlation structure, limiting their ability to capture realistic market dynamics for American option pricing.
AI.method: The authors generalize SLV models by adding stochastic correlation driven by an additional stochastic process, derive the corresponding reflected forward-backward SDEs, and solve them with data-driven numerical methods. They also perform a convergence analysis of the numerical scheme.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate the performance of the extended models and the accuracy and efficiency of the RBSDE-based approach.
AI.conclusion: The RBSDE framework effectively models the future evolution of the option price, enabling efficient pricing and hedging of American options under the extended stochastic-correlation SLV models.

title: An explicit formula for the solution of the Benjamin-Ono equation and its applications
